Title: [AI x Growth Workshop] Prompt Tracking is Bullsh*t. What 10,000 Hours of AI Visibility Taught Us. · Zoom · Luma

URL Source: https://luma.com/growthx-ai-workshop

Markdown Content:
​**Your visibility score went up. Your traffic didn't.**

​Prompt tracking was a reasonable first move. Build a list of prompts, get a score, watch it move. The problem is that the score moves on its own. Ask the same question twice and the answer comes back different. It can tell you that you dropped. It can't tell you why, or which page caused it, or what to go fix.

​Your buyers don’t think in prompts. They have something to figure out and they ask it however makes sense that day. The wording keeps changing. The question doesn't. Map the questions that matter in your market and the picture gets clear fast:

*   ​Where you already answer well,

*   ​Where a competitor answers better,

*   ​Where nobody in the category answers at all.

​That map is something you own and compound. A score is just something you watch.

​Marcel is walking through the five lessons that came out of two years running client organic growth systems for companies like Vercel, SentinelOne and Webflow, and the playbook we built from them. Hundreds of live content systems, tens of thousands of pages under management, 2.6 million AI responses recorded.

​**You'll leave with:**

​

→ Why ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI answers each reward different things

→ Which buyer questions earn citations, and which ones don't

→ Why publishing more loses to ranking better, and the page count that changes your odds

→ How to measure patterns instead of single days. 59% of what we saw cited appeared on exactly one of the days we looked

→ How to go from one buyer question, to the page that answers it, to the result that tells you what to do next

​Prompt tracking is bullsh*t. Don't just track the answer. Become the answer.

​**Leading it: Marcel Santilli, CEO and Co-Founder of GrowthX AI.** 15+ years building growth engines, from growth operator to CMO to founder, across Deepgram, Scale, ServiceTitan, HashiCorp, HP and IBM. He gave the short version of this on stage at HubSpot's UNBOUND. This is the full one, with the playbook!

Title: 61 Million Consumers Ask AI What to Buy. Then They Buy It on Amazon.

URL Source: https://forkast.news/61-million-consumers-ask-ai-what-to-buy-then-they-buy-it-on-amazon/

Published Time: 2026-09-23T15:22:13+00:00

Markdown Content:
Analysis

PYMNTS data shows 60% of AI-assisted purchases still close on Amazon — and a controlled test reveals consumers don't believe the alternative is equal, even when told it is.

![Image 1: A wooden wheel with two grooves - one deep and well-worn, one shallow and barely scratched - with a small faceless mechanical figure at the fork reaching toward the untested path while still resting in the trusted one.](https://forkast.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/61-million-consumers-ask-ai-what-to-buy-then-they-buy-it-on-amazon-1024x687.jpg)

Roughly 61 million American consumers now begin their retail shopping research using AI. They have swapped the search box. What they have not swapped is where the money goes. Six in ten AI-assisted purchases still close on Amazon, according to [new PYMNTS data](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/agentic-commerce-needs-its-febreze-moment/). The search routine changed. The reward did not.

This is the central tension in [agentic commerce](https://forkast.news/glossary/agentic-commerce/) right now, and it has a name borrowed from consumer packaged goods. PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster calls it the Febreze moment.

## The Reward the Industry Has Not Built

In the late 1990s, Procter & Gamble launched Febreze expecting a blockbuster. The product eliminated odors instead of masking them. It flopped. The reason was not the technology — it worked. The reason was that most people who needed it could not smell the odor in their own homes. There was no cue to reach for the bottle, and when they did spray, they noticed no difference. No cue, no reward, no habit loop.

P&G fixed the problem by changing what it sold. It stopped selling odor elimination and started selling the fresh-scent reward at the end of cleaning. Febreze banked more than $230 million in its first year after relaunch. The technology stayed the same. Everything around it changed.

Webster argues agentic commerce is stuck in the same place. The industry is selling smart, seamless checkout. Consumers are not looking for a new way to click a button. They are looking for a guarantee that when something goes wrong — wrong size, wrong seller, refund that never shows — someone will make it right. “Trust is what’s left after a habit has paid off so many times that you stop checking and second-guessing,” she writes. Amazon has spent two decades building that habit. The agent has not built it yet.

## What the Numbers Actually Show

A [PYMNTS Intelligence survey of 2,191 US consumers](https://www.pymnts.com/study_posts/the-50-million-consumer-migration-the-data-behind-retails-shift-toward-ai-discovery/) in August 2026 found that 23% now start their retail shopping research with AI. That is 61 million people. Average AI-assisted spend rose from $889 in June to $1,039 in August — up 17% in two months. The discovery part is working.

But the buying part is not moving. Sixty percent of AI-assisted purchases still complete on Amazon. Big box and department stores get 20%. Brand sites get 6%.

The most telling data point comes from a [controlled test PYMNTS ran](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/ai-takes-the-first-step-in-shopping-while-consumers-keep-the-buy-button/). Consumers were told the AI assistant would find the exact same item at the same price, with the same shipping and the same returns, from three places. Forty percent still chose the marketplace. Twenty-two percent chose the department store. Sixteen percent chose the brand.

When asked why, the top answer was easier or more reliable returns, at 37%. Better selection, 35%. Habit, 33%. Better customer service, 32%. They did not believe the alternative was equal, even when told it was. Behavioral economics explains why: losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains. A bad purchase costs money. A bad search answer costs only time.

OpenAI learned this the hard way. It launched Instant Checkout in September 2025 and discontinued it by March 2026. Only about 30 Shopify merchants ever went live. Walmart said purchases made inside ChatGPT converted at one-third the rate of those sent to its own site. The “smart and seamless” pitch failed because it described the status quo for someone who already shops on Amazon. It was odor removal for someone who could not smell the odor.

## Two Sides of the Same Gap

This consumer trust trap connects directly to the supply-side problem Forkast has been tracking. [Only 11% of SMBs currently qualify as agent-ready](https://forkast.news/only-11-of-small-merchants-are-ready-for-ai-shopping-agents/), according to the PYMNTS/Visa GDSI Merchant Edition. Only 15% of merchants have the structured product data agents need to evaluate what is being sold. Only 23% can distinguish AI-driven traffic from human users. Merchants cannot see the traffic, and consumers will not leave the familiar. Agentic commerce is stuck on both sides.

The infrastructure layer is arriving. [Stripe built full-stack agent commerce capabilities with 288 launches at Sessions](https://forkast.news/stripe-just-built-the-full-stack-agent-commerce-infrastructure-in-one-day/). The [merchant landscape is splitting](https://forkast.news/shopify-embraces-metas-muse-across-all-stores-as-amazon-blocks-it-and-the-merchant-landscape-splits-in-two/): Shopify opened its entire catalog to Muse and Shop Pay, while [Amazon blocked the agent the same day](https://forkast.news/amazon-blocks-metas-muse-agent-from-shopping-and-signals-a-new-tollgate-for-agent-commerce/). The plumbing is getting built. The trust is not.

Webster’s prescription is blunt: match Amazon on the bad day and beat it on the all-in price. “The intermediary can open the door,” she writes. “The reward has to be the merchant’s own.”

Sixty-four percent of consumers check who the seller is when they buy on Amazon. They do not trust everything on the platform. They trust the platform to fix it when things go wrong. That distinction — between trusting the seller and trusting the resolution — is the gap no checkout protocol has closed.

## What Changes the Equation

The payment networks are positioned to own this gap, if they can make the promise visible. Zero liability protections already made a generation comfortable shopping online. The chargeback is the original “someone will make it right.” [As Webster puts it](https://www.pymnts.com/credit-cards/2026/the-next-battle-in-credit-wont-be-for-top-of-wallet/), “top of wallet becomes top of agent.” The issuer that makes its guarantee travel with the credential wherever the agent shops — wrong item, wrong seller, refund that never shows — could make a brand site as safe to try as the marketplace.

There is a gap between what consumers say would move them and what the agent currently delivers. A saved digital wallet on a brand site would move 24% of marketplace shoppers. An AI assistant handling the end-to-end checkout would move 12%. But in the controlled test, the marketplace still won at 40%. That 20-point gap between the 40% who default to the marketplace and the 20% who say everything-equal would choose differently is the prize. It is what comes into play when consumers actually believe the alternative is as safe as Amazon. Today they do not, and a survey cannot make them. Only experience will.

Until that experience materializes, 61 million consumers will keep asking AI what to buy. And then they will buy it on Amazon.

McDonald’s began piloting a media network across 450 company-owned restaurants in the U.S. last month, the Golden Arches owner announced during its investor day presentation on Wednesday. The fast-food giant hopes to build the offering into a billion-dollar business by showing ads from other brands during moments when customers engage with its app, kiosks, menu boards and restaurants.

“Commerce media is one of the fastest-growing areas in advertising and is expected to [reach more than $100 billion](https://www.emarketer.com/commerce-media-lookbook/) in the U.S. alone by 2028,” Morgan Flatley, McDonald’s executive vice president and global chief marketing officer, said during the presentation. “It’s an opportunity to generate revenue for the system with little in the way of additional cost, no operational complexity and no disruption to our customer experience.”

Plans for McDonald’s Media Network [surfaced in media reports](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-21/mcdonald-s-is-testing-ads-on-its-menu-screens) earlier this week, and the formal announcement was among several marketing developments shared during the company’s first investor day since 2023. The event saw McDonald’s executives dig into a strategic plan that was unveiled in June.

McDonald’s marketing initiatives are part of a consumer-focused pillar of the plan that includes [creating brand-led content](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/how-mcdonalds-is-serving-up-culture-as-part-of-its-new-strategic-plan/821833/) and co-creating with fans to reach consumers in relevant and personalized ways. Flatley detailed how McDonald’s will leverage fandom for the brand, which she said captures approximately 40% of positive mentions on social media across leading QSR brands — more than its next three competitors combined.

“These fans are the foundation of our new marketing model, which includes engaging them in big global moments and building deeper individual relationships,” Flatley said. “We’re evolving exactly how we build our brand to be more efficient and effective at moving culture to support customers making us their first choice.”

### Fewer, bigger campaigns

McDonald’s three-pronged marketing approach includes running globally scaled campaigns that can be amplified by fans and creators, helping the brand spend less on paid media. The campaigns will be built on its own intellectual property, making its marketing more distinct and ownable, and will run on a simplified calendar that prioritizes fewer but bigger ideas.

“We’re roughly doubling our investment in longer-running baseline-building programs focused on core credentials like our brand, taste and quality, and value, while reducing the number of short-term promotional campaigns,” Flatley said.

Simplifying the marketing calendar was first raised during the company’s Q2 earnings call around the underperformance of the brand’s FIFA campaign. The rapid succession of campaigns around the World Cup, “K-Pop Demon Hunters” and its value menu was [cited as a drag on operations](https://seekingalpha.com/article/4929945-mcdonalds-corporation-mcd-q2-2026-earnings-call-transcript).

“As we continue to make the upgrade around the taste and quality of our food and drive consumer awareness of it… that’s going to be the gift that keeps on giving,” McDonald’s CEO Chris Kempczinski said during the investor event. “You actually become a little bit less dependent on [whether] you have the right movie property this month or … the right other partnership which creates a little bit of that boom-bust dynamic.”

During the investor event, McDonald’s demonstrated how its new marketing model works by detailing a recent global campaign, the [World Menu Heist](https://www.mcdonalds.com/ie/en-ie/latest/world-menu-heist.html), that brought beloved local menu items from around the world to other markets. The effort tapped into fan interest to both generate millions of views and thousands of comments across social media and spur incremental guest counts and sales — all by using the brand’s own equity and IP.

### Global efficiency

McDonald’s has seen the power of unique brand experiences [like the Grimace Shake](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/mcdonalds-grimace-shake-viral-tiktok-trend-q2-earnings/689218/), [Adult Happy Meals](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/mcdonalds-happy-meal-streetwear-millennials-Gen-Z/632742/) and Famous Orders before, but believes such campaigns will be even more powerful in the future as the brand steps up its menu and looks for global efficiencies.

“We worked with around 10 major partners for Menu Heist versus the 40 that would traditionally have been used if each market had to execute locally, reaching greater scale than any market could achieve on its own,” said Manu Steijaert, president of international operated markets.

*   A case study is a human story used to prove a specific angle.
*   Expert commentary and case studies solve different problems — an expert has studied an issue; a case study has lived it.
*   Journalists now video-call unfamiliar interviewees before running their quotes.
*   Finding sources is a numbers game — Edd estimates only 5-10% of people contacted cold on social media respond.

Experts are great, but a real person who’s actually lived through something is what makes a story land with a journalist and readers.

On this episode, I chat with [Edd Dracott](https://www.linkedin.com/in/edd-dracott/), whose agency, [Folc](https://folcstories.com/), helps PR and marketing teams find the people and stories that can breathe life into a campaign.

Edd spent nine years as a journalist at The Press Association (now [PA Media](https://pa.media/)), which is the UK equivalent of Associated Press.

We get into what actually separates a human story from a case study or expert commentary, how Edd uses OSINT and social media to track people down, why a single great quote can make or break a pitch, and how journalists are protecting themselves from AI-generated fake sources.

Enjoy!

![Image 1: YouTube player](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/knqVESNU5Vk/maxresdefault.jpg)

Below is a slightly edited transcript:

## What Are “Human Stories” in Journalism — and How Do They Differ From Case Studies and Expert Commentary?

**Edd Dracott:** A human story is just a story about a real person — it could be someone who’s won the lottery, or someone who was a witness to a traumatic event, or someone who’s got some sort of extreme health condition they’re talking about.

The key thing is it’s someone who’s real, someone who has actually had a lived experience, and they talk about that experience.

A case study is a human story, but what we’re doing with a case study is exemplify the angle of a story, or a specific subject.

Let’s say your angle is new government legislation and its impact, and you’ve got stats showing 50% of people are now struggling with their monthly bills.

What would be so much stronger is having a real person who can say, “My bills have been so bad, I’ve been defaulting on payments, I’ve been struggling to pay my mortgage.”

Suddenly it’s a whole different story.

Those become the headline, the top line — they give you the pull quotes you otherwise wouldn’t have.

They’re fundamental to telling those stories.

For PRs, if you’re able to offer that case study — rather than just sending a pitch that says “a survey we found showed X% of people do Y” — and you can also offer the people who do Y, who have a really great example of it, then all the better.

Expert commentary is from someone who has thoroughly studied an issue, whereas a case study is from someone who has experienced it.

With the mortgage example, that’s a mortgage expert versus someone who’s had difficulty with their mortgage.

Or you could have an interview with a doctor talking about a specific condition, and then the patient talking about their experience with that condition — that’s the differentiation between the two.

## What Inspired You to Start Folc?

**Edd Dracott:** My time as a journalist — nine years of it — was spent at PA, the Press Association, which is the UK’s national news agency.

For American listeners, it’s very similar to Reuters or AP — hugely respected, and when you put content on the PA wire it goes all over the place.

A brilliant place to cut your teeth in journalism, with some fantastic reporters there.

My specialism was finding people online — online news gathering, from pretty early on.

Over time I became head of social media, which involved being head of online news gathering and also verification.

Through that I covered everything from conflicts like Afghanistan and Ukraine — speaking to people from the front line who were impacted — to the COVID pandemic, where we found people who had sadly lost loved ones.

But also much lighter stories — we’d find someone doing a remarkable fundraising campaign on TikTok, for example, and that would become a great lighter piece for the papers.

After about a year as head of social media, I also became head of “real life,” which is honestly the best beat in journalism.

If you’re not aware of what real life is, it’s human interest exclusives — we’ve got a great interviewee, we’re going to tell their amazing experience, and put it into an article or feature about them.

It’s so much fun. Everything from remarkable health stories — a guy we chatted to who lengthened his legs, decided to grow from six foot to six foot seven — to a woman who had a stroke and woke up with an Italian accent.

That one got tens of millions of views because it was on ITV’s This Morning, the Daily Mail, TikTok, all that sort of stuff.

But one of the key frustrations when I was working as an editor was getting hundreds and hundreds of emails from PRs pitching something, saying “could we work on this story together,” and they wouldn’t offer a case study — or even worse, they would offer one, I’d get my reporter to chat to them, and the case study didn’t deliver on what they said it would.

That wastes everybody’s time.

So I was thinking, why isn’t there a service out there helping PRs get these case studies?

Because we do this every day — this is what I trained my journalists and my team to do. I taught them how to use social media, how to use open-source intelligence, which I’m sure we’ll talk more about, to find their own stories.

That was fundamental to everything we did on that desk.

It was always in my mind, and then I left PA partway through last year and went for it — decided to make that exact service.

That’s where we’re at now. We work with PRs and brand marketing teams and we source those stories.

We’ve essentially gone upstream in the news cycle, giving the case studies to the PRs, who then give them to the journalists.

It’s gone really well so far.

## How Does Your Social Media Background Connect to Finding These Stories?

**Edd Dracott:**Social media on one hand is fantastic for online news gathering, but it’s also such a great way of accessing an audience — it’s growing more and more.

Some of the PRs we’ve worked with have been amazing, and I’ve got to say, learning the other side — understanding the PR process, creating a campaign, making a pitch — has been really eye-opening.

A lot of what they do isn’t just sourcing a case study or an interviewee for a news story — it’s not just going for journalists.

It’s also thinking about social media — maybe this one isn’t going to go to a journalist, but we’re going to put it on the client’s Instagram or TikTok.

Or it might go directly on their website, because maybe we’ve just found a great customer who’s used the client’s service and made great use of it — has all the merch you could possibly get from them — so we go out, find them, and put them on the website.

Or it could be they’re not a customer, but someone who has the exact pain point that business fixes — we’ve found someone who goes through that experience, and the business could actually fix that problem for them.

That’s the absolute dream scenario.

Social media is fundamental to it, and it’s not easy.

It gets more and more difficult, and I think it’s becoming more specialized how hard it is to actually do the news gathering and use social media to source these stories, because AI has made it harder — there’s more fake content out there. It requires a careful, fine-tooth comb.

## What Are Some Examples of Campaigns You’ve Worked On?

**Edd Dracott:** Probably our biggest success so far — we launched this year — was Care Home Open Week in the UK. We did that as a partner of Big Bang PR, a small and mighty team up in Manchester.

The brief was: can we find World Cup–themed stories to mark the launch of Care Home Open Week, since it was happening at the same time?

Care Home Open Week is for a charity — it’s for championing social care and showing off the amazing work care workers do every day.

So that’s a big jumping-off point — lots of different ways in. How do you get a World Cup–themed story into a care home story?

What we found were 1966 World Cup final attendees.

We chatted to an amazing guy called Jeff Goldstone, who sat right behind the goal where Geoff Hurst scored his famous third — the “they think it’s all over, it is now” goal.

He said the ball was coming right towards his face before it hit the net — really great quotes.

We also found a ball boy from the final, Neil, a really amazing guy — he was the first Englishman to touch the ball in the final. If you watch it back, there’s a clip where the Germans kick the ball straight out of play, it falls right at Neil’s feet, he picks it up and passes it to one of the players. His line was, “If I hadn’t passed to that player, maybe we wouldn’t have won” — he takes credit for it.

Tying it into that brief, we had an event where we brought these people to a care home in London called Hendon Hall, which is also where the 1966 England team stayed during the tournament — so it adds to that history.

We managed to get BBC Breakfast to come along, which is the most-watched breakfast show in the UK, with over a million viewers each day — a really huge thing.

I found out afterward it was the client’s dream placement, which was great to hear.

We also got them into the Daily Mail and a few other outlets, plus BBC Online with a written piece.

Beyond that, we’ve had a lot of great stories.

One was Stephen Holt, a lovely guy who was born just after the 1966 final.

I found him through some searches on Twitter and tracked him down — he’s spent his entire life collecting memorabilia about the 1966 final because he’s obsessed with it; his family always told him it was the best thing that ever happened to England.

We got him to present his memorabilia to care home residents at another care home.

It was a really emotional thing — some of the residents are living with dementia, but they were able to recognize Bobby Moore and Bobby Charlton in the pictures.

We had the BBC there, ITV there, and PA, my old news agency, there, and his story ended up all over the place — the Daily Telegraph, the Mail again, Jeremy Vine on TV. A lot of great usage.

The last one from that campaign — we also wanted a Scottish story, since it was their first time going to the tournament in 30 years. We chatted to the son of a former Scottish footballer, Hugh Macklemoile, who sadly now has dementia and lives in a care home himself.

He was famous for his headers, so there’s a connection there — as you may know, there was an investigation from the Football Association in the UK into the impact of headers on dementia in later life, and part of his care is now paid for by the Professional Footballers’ Association.

That’s an interesting news line, and it went into the Daily Record in Scotland — the most-read newspaper there, online and in print.

To give you an idea of the range of what we work on — we’ve also worked with a holiday cashback service, talking about how you can make money from it, but they didn’t have an example of someone who’d actually done it.

We found a lady who’d saved a thousand pounds over two years and was able to buy her son an Xbox for Christmas — good fun, but it immediately humanizes the content of the release and the service they were trying to get across.

Right now I’ve also got a footwear company that wants women who’ve sadly hurt themselves in heels, for example.

It’s a real broad spectrum — essentially, as long as we’ve got a brief, we’ve got something to get our teeth into, and we can go out and look for it.

That’s the thing that really excites me.

My mission is to go out and find those things, and working on Folc is my excuse to keep doing everything I was doing at PA for years — just keep finding those stories.

## Why Do Great Quotes Matter So Much to a Story?

**Edd Dracott:** It basically entirely changes the impact of a story, because then you’re able to have a great headline.

Often a headline is a quote — there’s going to be quote marks in there, some great line pulled out of it.

I remember a person I spoke to after there was a strange power outage in the middle of London one year — all the lights went out, including all the traffic lights, for like 20 minutes, which was crazy.

All the headlines came from someone who said it was “apocalyptic” — that was every headline, because that’s what it felt like.

If you hadn’t managed to chat to that person, you wouldn’t have that line. But it’s what everyone was thinking as they saw it.

The other thing, particularly from a PR perspective — what makes something interesting compared to what you’d see on PR Newswire — is the offer of an exclusive interviewee.

Being able to speak to someone, full stop, as a journalist, lets you take ownership of the story, because you can ask your own questions and get your own quotes.

That completely changes how you approach it — you want to get that to the top of your piece, use the information you managed to get, and maybe you’ve thought of a way to relate it to the audience that someone else didn’t, because you asked a niche question someone else didn’t think to ask.

I remember — and I can’t believe I’m going to tell this one — a meeting with the former head of “real life” at PA, one of the first stories she had us work on, and it was with a nudist.

How do you make a story about a nudist relatable?

How do you make readers want to understand it?

She said: chat to them about the kitchen — how do they cook food?

It’s a risky business, right?

And suddenly you can paint the picture in your head — this is a much more fun piece, because you can talk about the little things they do day to day.

## How Do You Ask the Right Questions to Get Great Quotes?

**Edd Dracott:** I think it depends on the journalism you’re doing.

If you’re doing it for press, particularly a feature, you’ve got the luxury of maybe an hour for a long interview, getting information where you can, and maybe cutting in if they’ve given you a 30-minute answer.

But fundamentally, it’s about trying to get them to give you a one-sentence answer — if you can sum this up in one specific way, or describe this situation to someone who’s never experienced it before — then they play up to it, and they might give you something meaty.

**Vince Nero:** All right, let me try it. Edd, if you had to tell me the single most important reason people need human stories in their journalism, what would it be?

**Edd Dracott:** To give their stories impact, and to make sure the audience wants to read it.

The audience is readers — the audience is humans. If you can make it so that, from the very top line, a human reads it and thinks “that’s me, I can relate to that” — even if it might not seem relatable at first — that will give your story impact, and it’ll go really far.

That may not have been one sentence, but there you go.

## How Do You Actually Find These People Online?

**Edd Dracott:** There are a few key parts to it.

First, it’s about having the skills — do you understand how to use open source intelligence, for example? Open source intelligence is information you can access online.

I did a course with Bellingcat, the big OSINT experts, seven years ago now, and learned a lot from them.

Essentially, you can use skills like advanced Google searches, searching through social media in smart ways, Boolean search strings — there are a lot of different methods. It’s almost like coding, really, when you’re using Google in a certain way.

## Are There Any AI Tools That Can Help?

**Edd Dracott:** AI can be part of it, but in that fundamental first point of understanding the skills, it’s just another one of the tools you can use to access things.

You might use it to create a smart Boolean search string, which you then use in a search elsewhere.

The second part is creativity — you need to be able to get into people’s heads. That’s always the advice I used to give journalists.

For example, during COVID, when flights started taking off again after restrictions lifted, we thought: where is someone going to post about their flight taking off?

So we did a geolocated search to Heathrow Airport on Instagram, because everyone shows off that they’re going on holiday on Instagram.

You have to think in their heads — this is where they’ll post, and this is the kind of thing they’ll post.

And then it’s about tenacity — it’s ultimately a numbers game.

If you don’t have the skills and creativity to find lots of ways in — just like you said, if you got a message from some random person on the internet, would you respond?

Maybe 5%, maybe 10% of people will actually respond.

So the more ways in you have, the more likely you are to be successful.

A quick example of using those skills: when Ukraine was invaded, I got a call — at 5 a.m., not the best time to receive a call — from Richard Woodward, who said, “We need to find human stories from Ukraine, they’ve just been invaded.”

Within an hour I’d spoken to someone and we had quotes running on the wire.

It was a British-Ukrainian 19-year-old who had woken up to the sound of explosions — a really shocking story to cover.

How I did it was actually quite straightforward: rather than any fancy searches, I just thought, I need to speak to people who are speaking English and are in the right location.

So I did a long search of every different way you could say “I am in Kyiv” — spelled different ways, “here in Kyiv” — and went through all those people and chased them.

Eventually I found Valentina, an amazing person I’m still in contact with today, and her quotes ran on the wire.

It’s a specialist skill, and the thing I’d want to get across to anyone going into this is: it’s like learning the piano.

You can be told where the notes are, but you have to play it for a long time to actually get good at it.

If you’re a PR or a journalist looking to get into this, it will take a long time to get good and be able to access it enough to get really good results.

**Edd Dracott:** Disinformation is one thing they struggle with, because you have to be able to verify it, and that’s a lot to expect.

Journalists tend to be pretty good at verifying stuff.

But most of the journalists I’ve trained, if I’m honest, have never gotten brilliant at the actual searching, the news gathering part, because that’s not what they do every single day — if they’re on a beat where they’re mostly out on the ground reporting, they don’t have time to be constantly searching Twitter or Instagram.

So beyond battling disinformation, it’s also struggling with, “what’s my next search, how else can I find a way in” — because I’ve managed to find two people who’d fit the bill, but someone who’s been doing this for years might have found 20.

So it’s about how you find as many ways in as possible.

Another thing is properly looking at someone’s profile and assessing it.

What we learned through Bellingcat — the really high-end approach to verification — is that it’s not a binary process.

It’s about building a picture: if everything went wrong and my editor told me that was nonsense, we’re going to have to pull that story, what’s your argument going to be?

If you can give a really great argument, because you’ve shown this is everything on their profile — it locates them in this area, it all ties in well, they’ve got lots of posts that relate to it, we spoke to them, we got pictures of them in the situation, we got screenshots of them receiving cashback, for example, one of the examples we did recently — then you build that picture to make a good case that this is legit.

I was listening to your podcast with Rob Waugh recently — he did some amazing stuff on AI experts, and uncovered so many that were appearing in places like the Telegraph and the Times.

I’ve got a friend who works at the Times, and she was telling me all their interviewees now — if they don’t know the PR, they’ll always video call them to confirm they’re a real person before speaking with them.

Even if they know the PR and trust them, they’ll call the source themselves and get their quotes themselves — they won’t accept quotes just coming through secondhand, because of the way people have been burned on this.

So it is a process that diligent journalists follow — and there are so many brilliant journalists out there who really have to verify carefully.

My recommendation to PRs — from all the PRs I’ve spoken to, this has been a big headache for them.

Title: The SaaStr AI Guide to Building a Top-Tier Inbound AI Agent: 17,000 Conversations, ~600 Meetings Booked, and 60% More New Business

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/yRfHGq

Published Time: 2026-09-23T14:10:29+00:00

Markdown Content:
Our inbound AI agent has had 17,000 conversations with prospects in the last 12 months and booked about 600 meetings for SaaStr AI Annual 2026. And for 2027, it’s running almost 2x of the prior 12 months. Together with the newer self-serve agent we added on top of it, our inbound agents drove a 60% increase in new business. Three humans run all of this.

Amelia walked through the full build on the latest episode of The Agents. This is the step-by-step version: what we replaced, how the first agent is set up, and how we added the newest agents on top of it.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_4ArZ5j6tkA)

## What we replaced: a long form, a round-robin, and a one-day lag

Thirteen months ago, a prospect on the sponsor page hit a long contact form. It came to Amelia. She round-robined it to herself or David. Someone replied within about a day.

The reply was nearly always: _“Hey [company], you look like a great fit for SaaStr AI, let’s book a time”_ plus a Calendly or similar link. Amelia calls it the worst email on planet Earth. The prospect reached out to you, and the first thing they get back is a form letter. The team was slow to respond, and when they did, it was a soul-crushing generic response.

That’s the bar. Almost anything beats it, which is why the inbound agent paid off so fast.

![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.01.27-PM-1-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C940&quality=70&ssl=1)

## Part 1: The inbound agent on the site

### Step 1. Put the agent on your highest-intent page first

Ours lives on the **[SaaStr AI Annual](http://www.saastrannual.com/)** sponsor page. That’s where people who are already evaluating a ~$90K purchase land. We run it on Qualified, as an avatar called Amelia AI.

Start with the one page where a fast answer is worth the most money. Don’t start with your homepage.

### Step 2. Give it a real qualification job

The agent answers questions in real time, but its actual job is to _qualify_. Not in the lame “human kid fresh out of college” way that is a tax on the prospect’s time. No. In a way that in real-time, helps the prospect / customer too.

Ours works through in real-time:

*   Why they want to sponsor
*   Budget
*   What they’re buying for: lead gen, brand awareness, or speaking
*   Which competitors they’re watching or asking about
*   Exact examples of ROI of other similar companies

Every one of those answers makes the first human call better. Not a tax on waiting for someone to call them back, some day, some time.

### Step 3. Let it book the meeting on the spot

No handoff, no waiting for a rep to write an email. The agent books directly in real-time. This is the single biggest change from the old flow, because the old flow lost people in the gap between “submitted a form” and “got a decent reply.”

### Step 4. Open the call with what the agent captured. The humans are already ready to go and truly fully prepared.

When a prospect tells the agent what they want, we start the meeting there. A real example from the pod: _“You said you were interested in coffee and newsletters. Coffee sold out, but let me walk you through newsletters and the other things we have.”_

The prospect isn’t forced to repeat themselves, and the first ten minutes of the call aren’t painful discovery. Sales can just be there to truly help. And close.

### Step 5. Measure the full funnel, not the chat count

Our last 12 months:

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-11.44.56-AM-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C705&quality=70&ssl=1)

Some of those 17,000 conversations of course were goofball conversations. That’s fine. The agent doesn’t mind 😉 Meetings and closed deals are the numbers that matter, and we had real logos come through this path, including OpenRouter.

### Step 6. Know who this works for

This works because our sponsors and customers are tech-centric and increasingly AI-native. They do discovery on their own, talk to the agent, book their own meeting, and close. For those buyers, seeing an agent in the sales process is part of the evaluation. If you sell yourself as a top AI media / event property and the buying experience is a PDF and a two-day wait, they notice.

A non-tech buyer who’s happy scheduling a call two weeks out may not care. Know your buyer before you assume this transfers.

### Step 7. Don’t make it the only door

A real share of buyers will not talk to what is still an avatar, even if a well trained one. Some find it intimidating. Most just want the packages and the pricing without a conversation yet.

We debated killing the self-serve download entirely. We kept it, and that decision is what led to Part 2.

![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.02.26-PM-2-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C574&quality=70&ssl=1)

## Part 2: How we added the newest agents

For a year, the self-serve path was a download link to a Google Slides prospectus. It converted worse than the agent. The fix came from the agent itself: after we built our renewal agent, it told Amelia she already had most of the pieces and should do the same for inbound.

Inbound is more complicated than renewals because you know much less about the person. So everything below is about getting the most out of the little you do know.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-11.46.07-AM-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C596&quality=70&ssl=1)](https://youtu.be/_4ArZ5j6tkA?si=K9XiQqHtSDjz4XDF)

### Step 1. Replace the PDF with a tokenized page on your own site

Shorter form. On submit, the prospect gets their own version of the prospectus on our site, with a link unique to their company. Ours is built on Replit.

This matters because a static PDF tells you nothing after it’s downloaded. A page you host tells you everything.

### Step 2. Add heat mapping

We use Microsoft Clarity. We’d never heard of it. You probably haven’t, either. But 10K, our AI VP of Revenue, picked it as the vendor itself.

On the Base44 lead the pod walked through, the heat map showed time on the package overview, a little on Super Gold, most on Gold, then a long stretch on the contact form. He’d also told us in the form that he was interested in Gold and Super Gold, so the heat map confirmed what he’d said.

### Step 3. Wait 10 minutes before doing anything

Most self-serve visitors click off after 5 to 7 minutes. We set the wait at 10 so the session is finished and the heat map is complete before the agent starts working.

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-23-at-9.40.27-AM-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C672&quality=70&ssl=1)

### Step 4. Run first-party signals before anything else

The agent checks, in order:

1.   Have they been on the site (Qualified, Vector)
2.   Are they already in one of our outbound sequences
3.   Have they seen our recent LinkedIn or X ads
4.   Are they on the newsletter
5.   Have they attended an event
6.   Have they spoken at one
7.   Have we written about their company on SaaStr.com

Then competitors, which are the second-biggest signal. Third-party data comes after that.

The first-party layer is the part no vendor can sell you. On Base44, it surfaced that their CEO had previously come to SaaStr AI Annual, which Amelia didn’t know.

### Step 5. Route it everywhere at once

When the lead lands, the agent:

*   Emails Amelia
*   Pings her in Slack
*   Adds it to a live dashboard queue
*   Writes it to Salesforce, with the heat map and custom link attached

That last one used to be a quarterly manual Google Sheet upload. Ugh. Close to worthless.

### Step 6. Have the agent write the pitch, and a human approve it

The agent builds the narrative in 30 to 60 seconds: why this company should be at SaaStr AI, which of their competitors were at Annual, and recommended packages.

Use only public or anonymized results about other customers. For Base44, the pitch referenced that Replit was top of the leaderboard as the number one sponsor, which is public. Nothing proprietary about any customer goes into another customer’s pitch.

Amelia reviews, gives feedback if needed, and approves. The email goes out from her, not from a generic address.

![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.08.58-PM-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C992&quality=70&ssl=1)

### Step 7. Update the same link in place

This is the piece to copy first. The prospect downloaded something generic. After the pitch is approved, the same URL now opens with _“Marlin, here’s why Base44 should be at SaaStr,”_ with their competitors and packages in it.

Any time they return to the link, they see the personalized version. It becomes a living document you can keep updating for the whole sales cycle.

### Step 8. We built our own booker (although we didn’t plan to)

David used Calendly. Amelia used Read AI. Neither connected to anything. 10K suggested building our own, and it took the agent 20 minutes.

The booking link now shows the prospect’s company name, ties back to the prospectus they looked at, and tracks whether they opened it without booking. When someone bounces, the agent tells Amelia and drafts the next email.

The calendar looks like a minor detail. At 20 minutes of build time it was worth doing, and it closed the last tracking gap in the inbound flow.

![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.saastr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.11.48-PM-scaled.png?resize=1000%2C743&quality=70&ssl=1)

### Step 9. Route by who owns the most similar accounts. Agents with enough context are great at this.

Base44 went to Amelia, not David. Why? David owns Vercel, but Amelia owns Replit and Lovable, and the agent weighted that volume higher. When the agent can identify similar companies in your book, it sends the lead to whoever knows that type of customer best.

### The result on one real lead

Base44 inbounded, got the personalized follow-up, and replied that it was a great follow-up and fast. He immediately booked for Friday.

## What it runs on

*   **10K on Replit** as the backend: dashboard, queue, and the layer that writes to Salesforce
*   **Salesforce, run headless.** We rarely log into the UI. Any agent-friendly CRM with a strong AI will work.
*   **Qualified** for the on-site agent. Other products will work just as well.
*   **Microsoft Clarity** for heat mapping. We picked what 10K wanted 😉
*   **Our own booker**, built by the agent. Don’t do this unless ROI is high and it’s quick. Here, it was.

You don’t need to be an engineer to build this. We aren’t.

## Where this goes wrong

**Trying to build it all at once.** Build it stair-step. The on-site agent came first and ran for a year before the self-serve agent existed.

**Letting the backend app get too big.** For a few weeks 10K got noticeably worse. It told us it had too much in it: too much data, too many APIs. We cleaned it up and modularized, and the quality came back. Newer models help here too. Fable 5.1, which launched September 1, gives better advice on what to build and improve in a system this size.

**Forgetting the rest of the sales team.** Amelia works through 10K directly. David doesn’t have the same backend access, so he still logs into Salesforce more. The agent’s next proposal is a version of itself built for reps.

**Assuming one inbound path.** We run both doors in parallel today. The long-term goal is to merge them so everyone gets the personalized experience whether they talk to the agent or self-serve. We haven’t done that yet.

## The build order we’d recommend to copy us:

1.   The on-site agent on your highest-intent page, booking meetings directly
2.   Keep the self-serve path, and move it off a PDF onto a tokenized page you host
3.   Heat mapping and a wait window, but net net, all prospects get what they want (and are qualified) in real-time
4.   First-party signal checks, then competitors
5.   Agent-written pitch with human approval, updating the same link in place
6.   Potentially, your own booker, tied into all of it

We ran step one alone for almost a full year before adding the rest.

The human experience seems to be getting more important these days, not less.

**Here’s the thing: most sales interactions never felt all that human in the first place.** The standard is “pretty damn low” in the words of sales expert [Samantha McKenna](https://www.linkedin.com/in/samsalesli/).

Sam runs [#samsales Consulting](https://www.samsalesconsulting.com/), an all-women firm that has trained 320+ B2B teams how to get better at top-of-the-funnel sales, LinkedIn strategy, and executive branding. I’ve been digging Sam’s pro-tips on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/samsalesli/) and her [newsletter](https://www.samsalesconsulting.com/newsletter-signup/), which span everything from calendar etiquette to replying to a referral email to writing a great cold email. (I find myself applying these pretty frequently.)

Today Sam is letting me share her proven sales frameworks and pro-tips with all of you. What we’ll cover:

*   How to write cold outreach that gets a reply

*   Why you should try emailing execs over the weekend

*   The go-to agenda for an intro call

*   How to respond to the three most common buyer objections

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/de91882e-7179-4f22-8617-69140f79285f/Sam_McKenna_header.png?t=1789518394)

## How to write cold outreach that gets a reply

Everyone’s chasing the same silver bullet: an AI-generated email that feels 1:1.

It doesn’t work, according to Sam McKenna. At least not yet.

Even more important: your buyers are not only numb to it, they’re over it.

“The differentiator is being the one who actually makes the effort, not just appearing to make an effort,” Sam emphasized.

She recommends always starting with LinkedIn research, even if the buyer’s profile seems outdated. Look for common former employers, existing mutual clients, shared connections, and experiences you can authentically relate back to yourself.

It’s not enough to name the thing (“I see you went to Ohio State”). You need a real perspective on it, too: something you’ve read, experienced, or can genuinely connect to. Think: if I’m going to meet this person at a conference and need an ice breaker, what am I going to talk to them about?

Sam loves a funky subject line that breaks the traditional inbox pattern. Your goal should be to pique curiosity and signal effort before the buyer opens your email. Her rule: it should make absolutely no sense except to the person reading it. If you’re writing to Sam, you might consider “Switzerland + favorite Nickelodeon show + Bedoodle” (she’ll immediately know you did your homework).

AI does have a place for accelerating research, she clarified. Just not for generating the outreach itself.

Use AI to build a point of view on the person or company. Find where executives were recently cited, whether they spoke at conferences, whether the CEO keynoted their user event (and what the theme was). Use this as an input for your outreach.

The suggested email structure itself:

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/0b028013-b432-4cc0-adb9-36514e0e40c4/image.png?t=1789406922)

*   **Open with the authentic connection.** Reference what you found and say something real about it. The connection has to be genuine; a hollow name-drop is worse than nothing.

*   **Transition from human connection to pitch.**Most reps include an opener and then blow it; they pivot straight to “leading companies like yours are buying products like ours”. You need a bridge that stays buyer-focused: what challenge do your current customers have that you’ve solved for them?

*   **Frame the problem at the 300-foot level.**Make it concrete, specific, and immediately recognizable to the buyer. “Our analytics are world-class and can optimize your X, Y, Z” tells them nothing. Instead, name the specific, role-level problem: “You’ve invested hundreds of thousands in LinkedIn Sales Navigator licenses. Your team knows how to use them. They don’t know how to use them to sell.”

*   **Preempt the objection before they raise it.** Buyers are already objecting in their heads while reading; name it and get around it. This signals: I have a brain, I’ve thought about you, time with me won’t be wasted.

*   **Close with an implicit invitation.**“If nothing else, give me a reply and tell me to go fly a kite.” The buyer will respond because they respect the effort.

## Why you should try emailing execs over the weekend

Everyone sends outreach emails on Monday mornings at 9am, Sam told me. “You’re competing with a full inbox and a full week ahead.”

She recommends using Monday through Wednesday to write 50 researched emails. Save them as drafts. Then batch-send 50% on Thursday and 50% on Friday.

Weekends are for the follow-up email.

❝

“Executives are often working Saturday morning to close the loop and Sunday night to prep for the week (or because they’re already on a plane). **You’re reaching them when nobody else is making an effort, at the moment they’re actually thinking.”**

Sam McKenna

The second email comes within 48 hours of the first. It should be very short. Since you’ve already done the work in the first email, this email should serve as: “I sent you a really good email below. Can you read it and reply?” A short and simple, “Hi, seeing if you had a chance to read my below email - would be grateful for the chat, if you’re up for it” will suffice.

When someone agrees to a meeting, Sam has a strong opinion about calendar etiquette: don’t send a calendar link. She says a calendar link makes the buyer do the work; you want to take the work off their plate.

If you still disagree and think it’s more convenient, she’ll encourage you to consider this angle: Letting them book on your calendar means they’re scheduling around things you could move in the interest of speeding up the timing of the meeting. The best sellers will control every part of their process, not leave something like this up to chance.

What to say instead: “Feel free to send some dates and times that work, and I’ll schedule accordingly. Otherwise, here’s what my week looks like if that’s helpful.”

Offer wide blocks that include every internal meeting you can move. Nothing matters more than booking the meeting while you have momentum.

## The go-to agenda for an intro call

You’ve done all this work to land a meeting. Don’t squander it out of the gate.

The buyer arrives expecting a standard sales playbook. Maybe a chat about the weather. Perhaps there’s a 28-minute PowerPoint deck. Or you ask something generic like “what interested you in this call?”

Your job is to make every part of the call different from what they’ve experienced before. This begins with rapport-building from the first few seconds either using your research or from paying close attention (e.g., pull something from their background on the video call and ask about it).

Again, cleanly pivot from rapport to business. Most people either linger too long on rapport-building or cut it abruptly. Sam uses two seconds of silence to let the buyer fill the space, then makes her move. Her suggested line: “So,, listen, thanks so much for making time. I’d love to start here.”

Replace standard discovery questions (e.g., “what interested you in this call?”) with a structured framing of the call (e.g., “I could tell you a million things about #samsales, here are three: one, two, three”). Lead with the thing that got them interested, either from an inbound form or the pain you named in the email. Points two and three are cross-sell opportunities; related things they may not know you do.

Then immediately pivot to them. “I’d love to hear about you. I know X, Y, and Z. But tell me about your team and your initiatives for the year ahead, if that’s okay.” The buyer talks for 3 or 4 or sometimes 9 minutes, and that’s the point. “You know you’ve succeeded when they apologize at the end,” Sam advises.

You can now have a conversation between two human beings instead of running a rote qualification script. You might ask an open-ended question, active listening question, or a question behind the question. “The buyer has told you everything you need, and you didn’t have it drag it out of them.”

## How to respond to the three most common buyer objections

You could’ve done endless research and written the perfect email. Most people are still going to say no. But if you’re lucky, you’ll get insight into the reason why and be able to respond to it.

#### **Objection: “I’m not the right person”**

Sellers usually send a generic reply like “can you tell me who is?” This message signals that it’s the prospect’s job to figure it out, and it usually gets ignored.

Sam’s preferred structure:

*   Thank them for responding (a response is already a win).

*   Ask: “Would you be so kind as to point me in the right direction of who would be the right contact?”

*   Use EQ: “I realize it’s my job to figure this out, but your organization is so complex I could really use your help.” “Help” is a powerful word; people want to help.

*   Proactively offer to protect their identity: “Would you be okay if I used your name when I reach out? Totally fine if not — happy to keep you anonymous.”

You’re pre-empting every objection in their head: it’s your job, I don’t want anyone knowing I helped you, and I don’t want to get involved.

#### **Objection: “We just signed a 3-year deal with your competitor”**

The standard response here is no response. Sellers don’t reply, mark the opportunity dead, and move on.

Sam always replies and thanks them. “Thanks so much for the reply. I’d still love to stay in touch. If anything changes, let me know. I’ll go say hello on LinkedIn as well.”

There are a few reasons this matters. Other divisions may not be covered by the global deal. Things change, and a pilot opportunity may open up later. That buyer responded to you, which means they’re a warm contact (and they’ll probably change jobs).

Connect with them on LinkedIn, save them in Sales Navigator, and track their job changes. When they move, send another note: “Congrats on the new role. I’d love to talk about how we can help you here.”

#### **Objection: “We’re too busy, follow-up in a quarter”**

Sellers are told to push back on this, and try to get the next meeting booked immediately.

Sam disagrees. “At some point you have to respect their boundaries and what they’ve asked you to do.”

She sends this reply: “No worries. Really appreciate the guidance. I might send you a couple of notes leading up to that, and I’ll touch base in a quarter!”

Then she sets a real cadence of 3-4 touches over the next quarter. Touch 1 is in 1.5 weeks, touch 2 is 4 weeks after that, and touch 3 is 5 weeks after that.

Every nurture touch carries a POV and a specific value. Be consultative even when it doesn’t serve you directly. There should be no ask in the close of any nurture (they already know what you want).

❝

“We published this white paper. On page 13 specifically, you’re going to find something on go-to-market that I think will help you think about this differently. What I love about that perspective is X, Y, Z.”

The buyer often replies early on their own. You’ve now accelerated the timeline without a single “just checking in” email.

Sam’s guiding philosophy is to make an effort for the person, what she calls Show Me You Know Me® (SMYKM).

It applies from the first outreach all the way through a 10+ year client relationship. It applies everywhere including networking events, cold email, LinkedIn engagement, and conference run-ins when a proposal is already in the prospect’s inbox.

kept.article_text:
Title: Self-hosted social media scheduler — CogSend

URL Source: https://cogsend.com/

Markdown Content:
license MIT source open

Mastodon, Bluesky, LinkedIn, Threads and X. Write a draft, customize it per platform, then publish it now or schedule it. No subscription — it runs on Cloudflare's free plan.

`git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/deepakness/cogsend.git cogsend && cd cogsend && npm install && npm run setup`

Node 22.12+, a Cloudflare account, and five minutes.

Loading the demo…

[Video 3](https://assets.deepakness.com/cogsend/cogsend-demo-2k.mp4)

Features

Enough to run a presence on five networks from one place — with the delivery stats that tell you what broke, and none of the vanity charts you would never open.

Posts

Scheduled, published, failed and draft, with the account icons right there. Cancel or reschedule a queued post without opening it.

*    Per-destination results
*    Cancel and reschedule straight from the list

Insights

Published against failed, bucketed by your local days, with the same period before it alongside. Failures are grouped by reason, so a platform-wide problem looks different from one bad post.

*    7, 30 and 90 day ranges, in your own timezone
*    Failure reasons grouped, not a wall of API errors
*    Last post at a glance, so a silent week is obvious

*   Rewrite the post for X without touching the LinkedIn version.

*   Paste a long draft and it becomes a thread that fits the tightest platform you picked, counted the way each one counts.

*   Send it immediately or pick a time. Every destination carries its own status.

*   Retryable failures back off on their own — five attempts, then they park in Failed.

*   Up to four images per post, with alt text on each one.

*   See the card a URL will make while you are still writing the post.

*   Let scripts, Shortcuts and AI agents like Claude Code draft, schedule and publish with a personal key. It can never connect accounts or mint keys.

*   Settings shows the running version, whether the tick is arriving, and when a newer release is out.

Install

You need Node 22.12+ and a Cloudflare account with Workers, D1 and R2. Setup is the whole install.

1.   It creates the D1 database and the R2 bucket, generates the secrets, creates your account, applies migrations and deploys. Safe to re-run.

$ git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/deepakness/cogsend.git cogsend
$ cd cogsend && npm install && npm run setup 
2.   Read-only. It confirms the Cloudflare account, the database, the bucket, the secret and the deploy. Every failure prints the command that fixes it.

$ npm run doctor
# add -- --app-url <url> to ask the live app too 
3.   Open the URL setup printed, sign in, and scan the QR with an authenticator app. Mastodon and Bluesky connect straight away; LinkedIn, Threads and X each need a developer app of your own first.

Every command, flag and failure mode is in the [install and deploy guide](https://cogsend.com/docs/deploy/).

Questions

*   Nothing, for a personal instance. There is no subscription, nothing to cancel, and no account with us — you deploy it to your own Cloudflare account, on Cloudflare's free plan. A personal instance stays well inside it.

The one thing Cloudflare asks for is a card on file for R2, the bucket that stores your images. Workers and D1 never ask for one, and you are only charged if you go past the free limits.

*       *   Storage. R2 keeps the first 10 GB free, and traffic out is always free.
    *   Cron triggers. Five per account, shared with every other Worker you run. If they are taken, drive the scheduler from your own timer instead.
    *   The database. D1 pauses for the day past 100,000 rows written. It resumes at midnight UTC, and nothing is lost.

Numbers can change: [Workers limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/), [D1](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/pricing/), [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/).

*   No. Mastodon and Bluesky connect with what you already have. LinkedIn, Threads and X need an app you register with them first, because they issue the client id and secret your Worker uses — pick one and the app shows you exactly what to create.

X also charges for posting. Its API is pay-per-use, so fund a small balance before you connect it. See [OAuth app setup](https://cogsend.com/docs/oauth-apps/).

If you would rather not register apps, you can connect them [through Zernio](https://cogsend.com/docs/zernio/) instead. It has a free plan, though X needs a card there.

*   Yes. Your instance includes an MCP server, so Claude Code, Codex or any MCP client can draft, schedule and publish with your personal API key. A read-only key lets an agent look without posting. See [MCP server](https://cogsend.com/docs/api/#mcp-server).

*   Pull the new code and run the release script. That runs the tests, applies database migrations, rebuilds and deploys:

```
git pull
npm ci
npm run deploy:release
```

Settings tells you when a newer release is out. Your data is never in the repository, so a pull cannot touch it — posts, images and secrets live in your Cloudflare account.

*   In your Cloudflare account, in the database and bucket that setup created for you. Platform tokens are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, and the single admin account signs in with an authenticator app and backup codes. Nothing about your instance lives with us.

One clone, one setup command, and the Cloudflare account you already have. No signup, no trial, no monthly bill, and no one else holding your credentials.

`git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/deepakness/cogsend.git cogsend && cd cogsend && npm install && npm run setup`

[Read the install guide](https://cogsend.com/docs/deploy/)[Star on GitHub](https://github.com/deepakness/cogsend)
