Marketer’s Guide: 

# How to Win AI Search with Creators


What’s a cozy cabin destination for a weekend trip? Introduction 

# The consumer journey has changed 

You’ve typed your brand name into AI, compared what came back to a competitor, and closed the tab without a clear next step: check, worry, wait, repeat. Meanwhile, consumers aren’t waiting. AI has already become their go-to research tool, well ahead of most brands having any plan for what to do about it. 

# 86% of marketers have already manually checked how AI describes their brand — yet most have no system for what to do next. 

# 94% of marketers say AI research is already part of the customer journey, broadly or in specific categories. 

# 91% of marketers agree consumers are using AI tools to research products before purchase. 

## The answer? 

AEO. Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the process of optimizing your brand for AI search results. 

## AEO is already shaping up to be the next competitive divide. Introduction 

## What marketers are actually afraid of


Ask marketers what worries them most about AI search, and the answer isn't being absent from the conversation. Marketers’ biggest concern? Showing up inaccurately. 

# 85%  82%  61% 

Worry about inaccurate or outdated info  Worry about loss of narrative control  Worry about losing to competitors 

AI gets the brand's facts, claims or timing wrong 

AI cites sources the brand can't control and reshapes its story 

Rivals get recommended, or the brand doesn't appear at all 

Being described incorrectly is a trust problem, and trust is harder to win back once a wrong version of a brand’s story starts getting repeated. 

# 28% 

of senior marketers say AEO is already a near-term priority or an emerging opportunity they are monitoring. But things are moving fast. Brands need to move from passive monitoring to clear ownership, as early action can help shape AI visibility before competitors define the category. Introduction 

## The Four Pillars of AEO 

While AEO and SEO have many similarities, AEO answers sit across a wide breadth of content that’s distributed across the internet, not just concentrated on your owned website. Here’s what to take note of: less than 10% of what AI search says about a brand comes from brand-owned content, according to  McKinsey . 
Brands need to evaluate, prioritize, and invest across these four pillars to effectively impact how they show up in AI search:


# 01 

# 02 

# 03 

# 04 

Brand-owned content 

Web pages, blog posts, product pages, email newsletters, help-center articles 

Creator and UGC 

Creator posts (sponsored or organic), long-form YouTube videos


Earned media and editorial coverage 

Press coverage, news articles, analyst reports, industry publication write-ups 

Forum and community mentions 

Organic, unprompted discussion across niche forums 

# <10%  of what AI search says about a brand comes from brand-owned content, according to  McKinsey .Introduction 

## Why focus on creator AEO? 

The consumer journey in 2026 is heavily influenced by two key areas: recommendations from LLMs and recommendations from trusted creators. Dollar for dollar, you're going to get the most return investing in creators for your AEO strategy.  Why? Because you’re tackling two of the most impactful parts of the consumer journey with a single strategy. 

# 1 in 3  Later campaign findings, 2026 

AI answers cite creator content 

and it’s one of many sources that shape how AI describes a brand, alongside owned content and earned media. 

You could start to think of an LLM as its own form of an influencer in the purchase journey, and you can't ignore it. You have to spend time there. Otherwise, you're ceding to your competitive set who will probably start to take share of model away from you. 

Lyle Stevens 

> Co-Founder and Chief Strategy Officer AT L ater

Introduction 

## A playbook built from real campaigns  What are the best trail running shoes? 

We work with leading brands across CPG, fashion, auto, and retail as AI search evolves in real time, and we’ve been among the first to up-level traditional creator marketing campaigns specifically for AI search visibility. Most brands already know this is a problem; they're just missing the internal infrastructure and alignment to act on it. Our team helps bridge that disconnect.
 Terraventure Speed 

> Buy now

This guide focuses on the creator piece of AEO, because it's the lever most brands are already investing in to drive awareness, consideration, and purchases. A creator AEO campaign still delivers the same solid influencer content your brand would have run anyway. The unlock is that same content can also earn AI citations most brands aren't currently in the running for.


> Where should I go for a girls trip?

Chapter 01 

# Fixing internal team alignment 

## Where AEO sits across marketing teams today 

AEO ownership splits across six general functions, but 25% of marketers can’t name a clear owner. Even where ownership exists, it's marketing-owned as one of many responsibilities instead of a dedicated function.
 Alignment starts with shared prompts across 2 core teams: SEO owns the technical side of visibility while Creator teams own the relationships and the content AI is actually citing. 

25%  24% 

17%  15% 

10%  9% 

Unclear / Shared ownership 

Growth & Digital  SEO  Creator / Influencer/ Social  Brand marketing / PR & Comms  Content Marketing Chapter 01 

## What each team brings, and what’s missing 

SEO teams tend to treat AEO as a technical infrastructure problem: schema markup, structured data, and owned-content optimization. Creator teams run campaigns built for impressions and engagement. Both are doing their jobs well — but neither has a mandate to optimize specifically for AI citation. 

We've entered a new era I've never seen before, where SEO teams and creator teams are now working together. These are two ends of marketing that never had to collaborate before. What we love to do is partner with the SEO team leading on-site content creation, so the creator content ladders into what the brand is already saying on its owned channels. The biggest mistake we're seeing is brands copying and pasting their SEO strategy, focusing on their own content over third-party content. 

Cameron Miskho 

> Sr. Director, Strategic Consulting at L ater

If SEO owns the technical side of search visibility and creator teams own the relationships and the content AI is actually citing, the alignment begins with shared prompts. Start with a shared list of prompts to target, built by pairing your brand's existing SEO keyword data with the questions its customers are actually typing into AI tools. That means thinking less like a search strategist and more like an everyday person talking to an LLM. 
Because LLMs are trained on historical data, when they don't have your information in their training set, they essentially do a Google search. SEO is still important in this case, but if you're not in that initial training set, you're at an inherent disadvantage to your competition. This is where search prompts come in.
Chapter 01 

Picking those prompts is the hardest part of AEO, often harder than traditional SEO keyword strategy, because creator budgets are finite in a way SEO investment often isn't. A brand can't cover the whole funnel the way it might with organic search, so teams have to choose between top-of-funnel, educational prompts, and commercial-intent ones.

In practice, that means building a working list of 10 to 20 prompts across four categories: 

Buying intent 

1 “What’s the best [product category] for [use case]?” 

Competitor comparisons 

2 “[Brand] vs. [Competitor]: which is better for [use case]?” 

3 Features and specs 

> “Does [product] have [specific feature]?”

Broad category questions 

4 “What are the top [category] brands right now?” 

That list becomes the shared brief both teams build from. SEO informs which prompts matter, while creator teams inform who and what earns citation against them. By using this target list as a continuous monitoring framework, both teams can track real-time AI responses to spot and fix brand misrepresentations quickly, ensuring accuracy stays at the core of your AEO strategy.


> Buy now
> What are the most trending cowboy boots?

Chapter 01 

## Measurement both teams can agree on 

Measurement should also tie back to what marketers already care about, not just technical metrics, including:


What matters most to marketers in AI search 

Nearly all want more AI visibility. Beyond that, success splits three ways*. 

71% Brand accuracy and control 

Business impact on sales and traffic  58% 

45% Competitive positioning 

> *multi-select question

Alignment only holds if both creator and SEO teams are measuring the same thing. Share of model is that shared metric.


Share of Model  how often and how accurately a brand shows up across its highest-priority prompts. Chapter 01 

This measurement breaks down into three layers: 

## 1.  How often 

the brand shows up at all across AI search results 

## 2.  How accurately 

the brand shows up against a specific prompt 

## 3.  Source or mention 

whether the intended link appears, or it’s just a passing reference 

Our team has found a healthy share of model starts around 30% (Later campaign findings, 2026) for top-priority prompts, giving both teams a shared metric to work toward. 

> Help me meal prep easy weeknight dinners.

Chapter 02 

# Rethinking your creator mix 

AI models weigh authority, specificity, and crawlability over reach, and they weigh third-party content over brand-owned content by a wide margin. Picking the right creator mix starts with addressing what marketers think shapes an AI answer, and what actually does. 

## Perception versus reality of what influences AI 

Roughly a third of marketers believe their brand website carries the most weight in shaping how AI describes them. Independent research tells a different story.
If owned content isn't doing the heavy lifting, the creators talking about your brand are.


# 1 in 3  marketers believe their brand website is the most influential source for AEO. Chapter 02 

## The retrofit that doesn’t work 

Brands often assume their existing influencer roster can simply be retrofitted for AEO. But it can't on its own. AEO calls for creators with topic-specific authority, and that's a different casting bar than reach or engagement alone. Existing relationships still matter, and they're a good place to start conversations, but they're not a substitute for AEO-first picks. 
Marketers already have a decent read on which creator types matter most for AI search visibility, even without a formal framework for why. 
Types of creators marketers believe are the most valuable for AI search:


Channels and creator types both matter 

YouTube, LinkedIn, and Reddit stand out as the platforms worth prioritizing* 

> By platform / channel

YouTubers  39% 

LinkedIn creators / thought leaders  26% 

Bloggers  26% 

Reddit contributors  24% 

Substack newsletter writers  19% 

> By creator type

Everyday product users  39% 

Industry specialists  36% 

Product reviewers  35% 

High-reach social influencers  32% 

Practitioners or professionals  32%     

> 0% 10% 20% 30% 40%
> *multi-select question

Chapter 02 

Micro influencers and smaller creators, at scale, can also have an incredible impact. That was a game changer for us, thinking about LLMs looking for trust signals, meaning repetition and consistency. With one of our brands, whenever we searched anything related to it, one specific dermatologist kept coming up again and again, and she wasn't even someone we were working with. Her narrative was shaping what our brand showed up as in AI search. 

Carly Baron 

> Chief Commercial Officer at Advantice Health

## Three creator types for your strategy


A strong AEO-ready creator mix has three parts, each doing different work.


Attention 

Entertainment 

Authority 

Thought Leadership 

Answers 

Technical Depth  

> PILLAR
> Attention
> Authority
> Answers
> PLATFORMS EXAMPLE FORMATS
> short-form explainers • infotainment • professional video guides
> expert POV posts • long-form articles • in-depth guides
> reviews & comparisons • community Q&As • real world use cases

Chapter 02 

## Follower count doesn’t predict citation 

Brands are used to sorting their creator roster by follower count, but that number has almost no bearing on whether a creator's content gets picked up by an LLM. 

# 57%  of the YouTube videos AI cites come from channels with fewer than 100K followers 

> Later campaign data,

Nano and micro creators, activated at scale around the same topic, can build the repetition and consensus a LLM is looking for. This is good news for creator marketing budgets, as activating smaller creators at scale means your dollars go further. 

When evaluating creators, teams should look past follower count and instead look at: 

If they consistently cover the exact topic your prompts target 

If activating several creators together can build the repetition an LLM reads as consensus 

If their content lives somewhere crawlable (more on this in Chapter 3) 

If they already carry authority on the topic independent of their following Chapter 02 

## Case study: Putting creator AEO into practice 

Here’s how Later helped a major CPG fabric care brand reclaim the conversation in AI search. 

## Challenge 

AI results were giving consumers inaccurate information about one of the brand’s products. 

## Solution 

In partnership with the brand developing owned content to combat the false narrative, Later executed a creator AEO strategy by activating five expert creators to produce content backed by research and science, addressing the incorrect information and mirroring similar language to the brand. 

## Results 

Within one month, all the Later creator content was ranking in Google AI Overviews. That's the power of combining brand-owned content with creator content. It's not just about showing up when AI gets it right, it's about being able to correct the narrative when AI gets it wrong. The strategy drove measurable lift in brand mentions and citations. This helped improve brand perception and signified authority to the LLMs. Chapter 03 

# The activation playbook for creator AEO 

Most brands don’t need to start from zero when it comes to AEO. The new playbook is to take creator content already in motion, optimize it so AI can actually find it, then measure whether it's working.


1: Optimize existing content first 

Video assets have to be transcribed and hosted somewhere AI can actually read them. YouTube is the most effective bridge between creator marketing and AI visibility, but only when it's optimized with citation in mind. Content on Instagram Reels and TikTok can often sit behind login walls that block AI crawlers, so a great piece of content can rack up views and still never reach the models forming answers about a brand. 

## The fix  Pull the content transcript, upload it to YouTube, and build a landing page that links out to the original post so the content becomes discoverable on both ends. 

The uncomfortable part of AEO is that the signals AI trusts most are the ones furthest from brand control, so the fastest way in is through human experts who already have credibility and authority on your topic. Find the creators being cited in your category's AI answers today, partner with them on original, expert-led content, and measure performance on AI citation pickup rather than impressions. 

Kaleigh Moore 

> AEO strategist + B2B creator

Chapter 03 

## AEO short-form video checklist 

Why it matters What 

Prescriptive on-screen text  Include the question and answer into text overlays so models reading frames see the connection 

Full captions & transcripts  Upload complete, accurate captions so AI can parse the whole video 

Geo + query metadata  Write the title, description, and tags with the exact prompt the video answers 

2: Build AEO into the campaign from the start 

Once you’ve optimized existing creator content, start building creator AEO objectives into future campaigns. AEO should be a standard consideration alongside reach and engagement, rather than a separate work stream run after the fact. That means briefing creators with target prompts in mind from day one, and treating transcription, captioning, and cross-platform distribution as a normal part of the production process. AEO is another layer influencer campaigns can be built to achieve. Chapter 03 

3: Track share of model over time 

Measuring share of model involves regularly checking how often your brand shows up, how it's mentioned, and whether that mention comes with a citation, against the exact prompts both teams agreed matter most.


# 1.  Run each priority prompt through major AI tools

kept.heading: HOW GOOGLE AND UBER MEASURE WHAT CANNOT BE RANDOMIZED (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Major marketing investments that can't be randomized still need causal measurement, rather than post-hoc narratives. Google's CausalImpact and Uber's synthetic control methods show how you can estimate the effect of national launches, sponsorships, and other whole market interventions by building counterfactuals from historical data or comparable markets. These methods are weaker than randomized tests, so you should preregister the analysis, establish a strong pre period, run placebo tests, and report uncertainty intervals. Synthetic control should be a last resort for spending that cannot support randomization.
kept.article_text:
Title: How Google and Uber Measure What Cannot Be Randomized

URL Source: https://karandhir.substack.com/p/how-google-and-uber-measure-what

Published Time: 2026-09-16T18:01:02+00:00

Markdown Content:
There’s a category of marketing decision that sits above every measurement design I’ve covered so far, defined by one structural property: everything gets treated at once. A national launch goes everywhere on day 1, because staging it regionally would sacrifice the launch moment that justifies the spend. A major sponsorship airs to the whole country simultaneously. A rebrand can’t be shown to half the market without ceasing to be a rebrand. A price change can’t be concealed from a control group that shops in the same stores and talks to the same people. These are routinely the largest individual line items in a marketing plan. And they’re structurally immune to both the A/B test and the geo holdout, because when the treatment covers the whole population, there’s no unit left to hold out.

The default measurement of these moments, at most organizations, is narrative. The campaign ran, the business performed, and a story connects the two, delivered with conviction by whoever owns the spend. The story survives because nobody in the room holds an instrument capable of checking it. My argument this week: the instruments exist, they were built and published by some of the best measurement organizations in the world, and what separates using them from settling for narrative isn’t statistical capability. Any leader can enforce the difference without writing a line of code.

_The Instrument Family_

The founding method is synthetic control, introduced to the economics literature by Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller in a 2010 study estimating the effect of California’s tobacco control program. The problem structure was exactly the marketing problem. One unit, California, received the treatment. No comparable unit could be randomized. The question was what California’s smoking rates would have been without the policy. The method’s answer: build a synthetic California, a weighted blend of other states chosen so the blend tracked real California closely in the years before the intervention. The gap between real California and its synthetic twin after the policy is the estimated effect. The logic generalizes to any setting with one treated unit, a donor pool of untreated comparators, and a clean pre-period.

Google industrialized the time-series version of this logic for advertising. CausalImpact, published by Brodersen and colleagues in the Annals of Applied Statistics in 2015, uses Bayesian structural time-series models to build the counterfactual. It learns the relationship between the treated market’s outcome and a set of control series during the pre-period, projects that relationship forward through the campaign window, and reads the effect as the gap between observed and projected, with credible intervals that widen honestly as the projection extends. Google built it because advertisers kept launching interventions that couldn’t be randomized and kept asking what the interventions did.

Uber operationalized the same family under marketplace constraints. The company has said publicly that its experimentation platform runs more than 1,000 concurrent experiments across 4 methodological families, with synthetic control and difference-in-differences sitting alongside classic randomized tests as first-class citizens. The reason is structural to their business. When an intervention touches an entire city, network effects between riders and drivers make within-city randomization meaningless, so Uber treats whole markets as units, constructs synthetic controls from donor cities, and presented the framework publicly, including a dedicated PyData Amsterdam talk in 2019 on causal inference when A/B tests are not possible. And when even city-level holdouts fail? Uber alternates treatment and control over time within a single market, switching on a cadence of roughly 160 minutes, so a 2-to-4-week test accumulates hundreds of experimental units from one city. Netflix, as covered earlier in this series, extended the same model family in its internal Quasimodo tooling, with a multivariate structure that reads multiple interventions across multiple regions.

The lineage matters. The hardest measurement problem in marketing has a published, replicated, industrialized solution family, built by companies whose measurement teams had no tolerance for stories.

_What Separates the Instrument From the Story_

Let me be blunt about the weakness first. Synthetic control methods are weaker than randomization, and pretending otherwise discredits them. The estimate depends on modeling assumptions rather than the physical act of random assignment, which means the method can be bent into producing whatever its operator hoped to find. The entire value of the family rests on disciplines that constrain the operator. Those disciplines, and they aren’t mathematics, are what a leader should inspect.

Pre-registration comes first. The counterfactual model, the control series or donor pool, the outcome metric, and the analysis window get specified and documented before the intervention launches. A synthetic control analysis constructed after the results are visible is a retrofit, and a retrofit will find what its author needs it to find, because donor pools and model specifications offer enough degrees of freedom to manufacture nearly any conclusion. One question exposes a retrofit: show me the analysis plan, with a date on it, from before launch. No dated plan? That’s narrative with equations.

Then the pre-period standard. The method’s authority comes entirely from how well the counterfactual tracked reality before the intervention. A launch measured with 3 weeks of clean history has almost no authority. Netflix’s public candor here is instructive. When they promote a title before its launch date, the outcome metric has no pre-period at all, because nobody can watch a show that doesn’t exist, and rather than letting a time-series method fail politely, the team switches designs entirely. Declaring a method inapplicable is a maturity marker. The executive version of the standard: no pre-registered pre-period, no causal claim.

Third, the placebo test. Run the identical analysis on markets that received no treatment and on dates when nothing happened. If the machinery finds effects in placebo cases at anywhere near the rate it finds them in real cases, the machinery is measuring noise, and every result it has produced deserves a haircut. Placebo testing is cheap and standard in the academic literature. Marketing organizations almost never demand it, which tells you something about what those organizations want from measurement.

Last, interval honesty. The output of a structural time-series counterfactual is a distribution, and the credible interval is the finding. A team that reports the point estimate and buries the interval converts a probabilistic read into false certainty, and a leadership audience that rewards narrow-sounding answers is training its measurement function to lie with precision. The interval on a synthetic control read will usually be wide. Wide is the truth. The fair comparison isn’t against the false precision of attributed numbers. It’s against the alternative actually on offer for these moments, which is a story with no interval at all.

_The Rule on Unmeasurable Spend_

I run measurement for a $1B portfolio, and the synthetic control family occupies a specific, bounded seat in that system. Instrument of last resort. Reserved for strategic moments where randomization is structurally impossible. Operated under the 4 disciplines. Never permitted to substitute for geo experiments on channels that could have been held out. The bounded seat is what keeps it honest, because the moment quasi-experimental reads become the default instrument rather than the last resort, the organization has opted out of randomization wherever randomization is merely inconvenient. Which is everywhere.

Here’s the rule I hold, and the one I’d put in front of any leadership team. Spend that can’t be measured by randomization and can’t support a disciplined counterfactual is spend whose impact is unknown, and unknown should be said out loud, in planning documents, in exactly that word. Unknown is a legitimate status. Portfolios legitimately carry strategic investments whose returns can’t be estimated with rigor, and mature leadership funds some of them anyway, on conviction, with eyes open. What corrodes a measurement culture isn’t the existence of unmeasurable spend. The corrosion comes from laundering unmeasurable spend through analyses that simulate rigor, because every laundered number teaches the organization that the difference between evidence and decoration is negotiable.

The companies that built these instruments share something that has nothing to do with engineering budgets. Google published CausalImpact into the statistics literature. Uber presented its synthetic control framework in public. Netflix documented where its own methods fail. Each decided the moments that matter most deserved better than stories, then held its own analyses to the standard that decision implies. The mathematics is downloadable. The discipline is the differentiator.

Title: Is the Traditional Marketing Team Dying, Shrinking, or Turning Into Something Else?

URL Source: https://www.kieranflanagan.io/p/is-the-traditional-marketing-team

Published Time: 2026-09-18T11:12:43+00:00

Markdown Content:
After “[Is the CMO role dying?](https://www.kieranflanagan.io/p/the-cmo-role-is-dying-heres-why-i)”, the number one question I get asked most is what happens to the marketing team. How drastically will it change? And is it going to shrink in size?

In May, I published a first draft of an answer: [how to rebuild your marketing team for the agentic age](https://www.kieranflanagan.io/p/how-to-rebuild-your-marketing-team). It consisted of four layers. Context, Execution, Orchestration, Leadership. At the time, I said it was a work in progress.

This post is the evolution. I’ve talked to a lot of other AI-native leaders about what they’re seeing happen with the traditional marketing team. I’ve gone from that original model to a set of beliefs. These are 3 principles I think every future marketing team gets built on, and something you can use to start on each one this week.

Here’s what’s happening today: every founder wants marketing to do more, with less. Gartner’s 2026 CMO survey says 39% of CMOs plan to cut labor and agency costs. Boards across tech see AI and ask the founder/CEO: why does marketing still need the same headcount?

Gartner’s 2026 CMO survey says 39% of CMOs plan to cut labor and agency costs. Boards see AI and ask why marketing still needs the same headcount.

The same survey shows companies are spending more on marketing headcount, from 21.9% to 24.5% of the marketing budget. What’s interesting is Martech, e.g., actual tools, fell to 19.4%, a five-year low.

Then look at who’s winning. Emily Kramer analysed 100 of the fastest-growing B2B companies. 87 have open marketing roles. 507 roles in total. Every company that has raised over $500M is hiring marketers. Marketing holds steady at about 4% of headcount.

So, the narrative is marketing teams should be shrinking, but the best companies are hiring. The reality is the team is changing shape, and most of the debate online is about size.

Here’s the shape I believe in.

For forever we’ve built marketing teams out of specialists. A plethora of people with a specific domain expertise. A paid person, an SEO person, a PMM, a brand person. It’s been that way because humans can only hold so much context. That limits how much action they can take. It’s constrained by context.

Today, I’m seeing super generalists, powered by their own AI system, collapse all that expertise into an AI-pilled process. They can take an idea from nothing to shipped v1: the research, the positioning, the page, the campaign, the data analysis, all on their own. No handoffs. They’re a generalist, and what makes that possible is the system they work inside.

Every great personal AI system has 4 core parts. I’ve explained these in previous posts. **Context** is what you know: your market, your customer, your voice, what’s worked. **Connections** are the tools and data the system can reach. **Skills** are your playbooks, written down so an agent can run them. **Artifacts** are what ships.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!p4nn!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2c972f2e-cf7d-4e08-997a-e229bed8bfa2_2912x1632.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!p4nn!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2c972f2e-cf7d-4e08-997a-e229bed8bfa2_2912x1632.png)

The critical thing in an AI system is the arrow back. The results write into Context, so the system gets smarter every time you ship. Back in May, I called this a loop. Today, loops are a common part of how we speak about AI.

We already see this role live in the market. Ramp has an “Agentic Operator, Growth Marketing” role. Cursor is hiring a “Marketing Systems Lead”. 84% of marketing job descriptions now mention AI. This is principle one on the changing shape of marketing teams.

Here is your homework. Unlike what most people are giving you, there is required work from you. AI is making people lazy. But, the best outcomes are still derived from your work.

**Your takeaway: build your v1.** Paste this into Claude:

```
You are helping me design v1 of my personal AI marketing system.
It has 4 parts: Context (what I know), Connections (the tools and
data I can reach), Skills (repeatable playbooks), Artifacts (what ships).

Interview me one question at a time. Ask about:
1. My role, company, and the outcome I'm accountable for
2. The 3 jobs I repeat most often
3. The tools and data sources I use each week
4. The best work I've shipped in the last year, and why it was good

Then give me a one-page system map:
- Context: the 3 to 5 files I should write first, one line on each
- Connections: the 2 tools to connect first, and what each adds
- Skills: the first 3 skills to build, in order, with input and output
- Artifacts: what each skill produces and where it ships
- The loop: which results get written back into Context

Keep it to what I can build in 2 weeks. Flag anything that needs
my judgment, not the model's.
```

Why do our existing org charts look the way they do?

The first org chart was drawn in 1855 to run a railway.

Daniel McCallum had just taken over the New York and Erie, nearly 500 miles of track and one of the longest systems in the world. A new technology, the telegraph, was flooding him with reports of delays and accidents. He had plenty of information. What he didn’t have was anyone clearly responsible for acting on it. So he drew a chart of who answers to whom.

It was shaped like a tree. The tree was built to move information around the organization. We’ve kept hold of that structure much longer than we should have, especially in marketing.

Every marketing team I’ve worked in has been some version of it. A leader at the top, channel owners underneath, specialists under them. Work travels up one branch, across, and down another.

That’s no longer how things work.

In an AI-native team, information flows through shared context in seconds. So the shape of the marketing team can change.

If one marketer can take an idea from 0 to 1, the team around them starts to look like a product team. Product and engineering worked this out years ago. Small teams. Each one owns an outcome. They ship every week, learn what worked/what didn’t, and go again.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OFIh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbc2eaeee-bfef-47d1-bd53-5bb8be1893e0_2912x1632.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OFIh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbc2eaeee-bfef-47d1-bd53-5bb8be1893e0_2912x1632.png)

**Your takeaway: the Pod v1 charter.** Don’t reorganise the department. Run 1 pod for 6 weeks, on 5 rules.

**One outcome.** Give the pod a result to own, like grow pipeline by x%.

**One named owner.** They make the calls and carry the number. This is the part most teams struggle with. The DRI has to be able to give people in the pod real orders, real direction.

**Super generalists.** Pods consistent of 0-1 marketers and marketers with real depth of marketing craft (see principle 3).

**One shared Context.** The pod reads from and writes to the same files. This is what replaces the branches of the tree.

**Ship and review weekly.** Demo what went live. Write what you learned back into Context.

The first two principles can sound like an argument for a team of generalists. This third one is the one I feel most strongly about, and I likely undersold it in my original post.

Depth of marketing craft will matter more than ever.

That seems counter to the principles above. But all marketing teams will have 0-1 marketers, powered by AI systems. The core structure will be pods vs. trees. But the depth of marketing craft will matter more than ever. And I want to show you how those things sit together.

Take product marketing.

A 0-1 marketer with a good system can now cover a surprising amount of the PMM job. They can build a launch skill that turns a product brief into the messaging doc, the launch plan, the enablement deck and the release notes. They can run a skill that reads every customer call and pulls out the words buyers use. They can keep competitor battlecards current without anyone asking. They can get a first draft of positioning on the page in an afternoon. Idea to shipped v1, across most of the function.

That work used to eat a PMM’s week. There is so much they had to do.

But some parts of PMM have been drastically elevated in importance. The positioning that makes a buyer stop scrolling. The tier 1 launch the whole company rallies around, and the market takes notice of. The story that gets repeated by your ideal customer. The first draft gets you to good. Getting from good to great takes someone who has spent years learning what great looks like in that one discipline. They have the taste and judgment necessary to excel in those critical aspects of the role.

The system handles the volume, which hands the expert their time back. A great PMM used to spend most of the week producing. Now they get to spend it on the part only they can do.

And it runs the other way too. Everything the expert knows goes back into the system. Their positioning becomes Context. Their launch playbook becomes a Skill. Their eye for a weak headline becomes the bar every Artifact has to clear. The next first draft starts from a higher place, for everyone in the pod.

This is why the pod charter asks for people with different spikes. Everyone in the pod is a 0-1 marketer. Each one is also the person the pod turns to for depth in one craft.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k5zk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5756224f-6848-4d4a-9ff1-f6fd053801e7_2912x1632.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k5zk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5756224f-6848-4d4a-9ff1-f6fd053801e7_2912x1632.png)

Production is now free. Work that stands out is scarce, and it comes from people who are deep in their craft.

**What I’d tell a marketing leader**

Build your own v1 first. You can’t redesign a team around a way of working you haven’t tried.

Run 1 pod for 6 weeks before you touch the org chart.

Plan to hire for super generalists and depth of craft.

Decide where you need great. Then make sure that expert’s knowledge is written into Context and Skills, so the whole team starts from their level.

And protect the juniors. Entry-level postings are down about 35% since 2023. Deep craft takes years to build, and if nobody gets those years, Principle 3 has no future. This is a hard one to solve.

**So is the marketing team shrinking?**

I don’t think so. It’s changing shape. It’s combining the 0-1 marketers & their systems, with depth of craft, all run through pods.

Until Next Time,

Happy AI’fying

Kieran

The annual [Made on YouTube event](https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/innovation-youtube-era-made-on-viewers-creators/) has just wrapped up, offering an early look at the features you can expect to come to Google’s dominant online streaming platform in the coming months. Yes, there’s plenty of AI for both viewers and creators, but there’s also a handful of non-AI updates mixed in there, too.

The design of YouTube’s homepage feed comes under fire often, but the platform is preparing to give you more options. With Custom Feeds, you’ll be able to add new tabs to the YouTube interface with content of your choice. To create a feed, just type a description and let YouTube populate the page. You can refine your description and rate video suggestions to tune the Custom Feed. Google says you’ll be able to save “multiple” feeds without specifying the exact number. This feature will roll out soon in the US for web, mobile, and TV users.

Interacting on YouTube will also change later this year. The platform will finally add the option to post GIFs in comments, which has apparently been a common request for some time. The comment box will let you search for popular animated thumbnails and post them on both regular videos and YouTube Shorts. The YouTube direct messaging feature is also adding support for group chat, but it’s only going to be available in the US, UK, Singapore, Brazil, and some European countries to start.

kept.heading: EVEN AMERICANS WHO USE AI EVERY DAY ARE WORRIED ABOUT IT (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: In Gallup's survey of 37 countries, the US was the most anxious, with 74% worried and only 36% expecting AI to mostly help the country.
kept.article_text:
Title: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/23/even-americans-who-use-ai-every-day-are-worried-about-it/

Published Time: 2026-09-23T16:49:58+00:00

Markdown Content:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations.

But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently.

Coming at a time of [intense debate](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/27/openais-hugging-face-breach-has-reignited-the-debate-over-alignment-and-control/) around the [dangers of AI](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/12/anthropic-ceo-outlines-plan-to-pace-the-frontier/), quick [developments around AI safety](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/15/openai-anthropic-google-have-been-in-talks-on-ai-safety-for-weeks/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the implications of [AI going rogue](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/09/gambling-with-our-lives-anthropic-researcher-quits-warns-against-self-improving-ai/), and accusations of [anticompetitive behavior](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/12/technology/doomsday-discussions-ai-companies.html), these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.

Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor are Australia and Malaysia.

The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% of Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.

Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them.

There’s certainly been a growing wave of [discontent around AI](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/17/if-youre-giving-a-commencement-speech-in-2026-maybe-dont-mention-ai/), with tech companies [laying off hundreds of thousands of employees](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/25/the-running-list-major-tech-layoffs-in-2026-where-employers-cited-ai/) in order to invest in AI, [shrinking entry-level openings](https://www.reveliolabs.com/news/macro/is-ai-responsible-for-the-rise-in-entry-level-unemployment/), life-ending [cases of AI psychosis](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/meta-ai-chatbot-death/), and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who [warned](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/27/dario-amodei-warns-ai-cause-unusually-painful-disruption-jobs.html) that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.

The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. In China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.

Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel, and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.

Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%), and Kenya (87%).

It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics [on the table for discussion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/23/trump-xi-meeting-ai-safety-chips-us-china-dialogue.html) when U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping meet on Thursday.

Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a [recent article](https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/jsc97cKVYOcHuI_WisvOxw) that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”

“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch.

While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education, or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.

At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.

kept.heading: CHATGPT ADS SEEM TO LIFT ORGANIC TRAFFIC. IS PAYING TO BE FOUND THE FUTURE OF AI SEARCH? (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: ChatGPT ads appear to coincide with higher organic ChatGPT traffic, but some of that lift may come from ad clicks being misclassified as organic referrals in GA4. OpenAI says ads don't influence its answers, and there is no public study proving whether ads affect organic visibility. It recommends tagging ad URLs, auditing ‘oppref' traffic, running holdout tests, and tracking organic mentions separately from traffic.
kept.article_text:
Title: ChatGPT Ads Seem to Lift Organic Traffic. Is Paying to Be Found the Future of AI Search?

URL Source: https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/chatgpt-ads-organic-traffic

Published Time: 2026-09-26T20:14:41.738Z

Markdown Content:
Marketers who have been running ads in ChatGPT for the past few months have started comparing notes, and the same pattern keeps coming up. When the ads are on, "organic" traffic from ChatGPT goes up. When the ads go off, it drops.

The accounts being shared on LinkedIn are specific. One advertiser reported a fivefold jump in organic ChatGPT traffic while ads were running, followed by a drop on the same day the campaign was paused. Another team testing the channel with a few hundred dollars saw almost nothing in the ad dashboard and was ready to cut it. Then they checked the CRM and found the client's largest potential deal of the year, sourced "organically" through ChatGPT.

For anyone who has worked in search, the suspicion is familiar. Google has been accused for years of rewarding advertisers in its organic results. Now some marketers wonder if ChatGPT is doing the same thing. It's a suspicion LinkedIn users already hold about their own feeds, where the reach that disappeared [is now being sold back to them](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/linkedin-organic-reach-pay-to-play).

The marketers raising this are careful to say they can't prove it. Maybe people see an ad and come back by name a week later. The data available inside the ad platform can't tell them which.

## What OpenAI says

OpenAI's position hasn't changed since launch. Its [help center](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001047-ads-in-chatgpt) says ads do not influence ChatGPT's answers, that they run on separate systems from the chat model, and that advertisers have no ability to shape or rank responses. Ads appear beneath the answer with a "Sponsored" label. OpenAI also decides who gets to buy that slot at all, and it can [shut out advertisers it considers competition](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/chatgpt-ads-competitor-ban).

There's no evidence OpenAI is misrepresenting how the system works. There's also no way for an advertiser to verify it. [During the current test](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001047-ads-in-chatgpt), advertisers get aggregated numbers like views and clicks and see nothing about the conversations their ads appeared in. When organic traffic moves in step with ad spend, marketers are left to guess at the cause, and "the answers are for sale" is the easiest guess to reach for.

There are at least four ways to explain what advertisers are seeing, and some fit the evidence much better than others.

## Ad clicks may be showing up as organic traffic

The least exciting explanation also matches the evidence best.

When ChatGPT links to a site in an answer, it adds `utm_source=chatgpt.com` to the URL, and Google Analytics 4 records the visit as a chatgpt.com referral. That's the line most teams now report as organic AI traffic.

ChatGPT ad clicks don't arrive with a channel label of their own. OpenAI attaches a click ID called `oppref`, which GA4 doesn't treat as a source. As [Improvado has pointed out](https://improvado.io/blog/chatgpt-ads-measurement), an ad click without the advertiser's own UTM parameters lands in GA4 as an ordinary chatgpt.com referral, sitting in the same bucket as a free mention. Unless someone tagged the campaign, paid traffic inflates the organic number from the first day.

Go back to the reports. Traffic climbs when ads start and falls on the same day they stop. Brand recall doesn't behave like that; it fades over weeks. A mislabeled paid channel behaves exactly like that. When a fivefold lift in organic traffic switches off overnight, the likeliest cause is ad traffic that was never labeled as ad traffic.

## The ad can start an organic conversation

OpenAI has also built a direct path from one layer to the other. Users can open the menu on an ad and select [Ask ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001047-ads-in-chatgpt), which shares the ad with the model so it can answer questions about it. OpenAI says advertisers have no say in those answers, and there's no reason to doubt that. Still, the conversation that follows is about the advertiser, and any link ChatGPT includes in its reply carries the standard organic tag.

You could argue that traffic is organic, since the model decided to link. It also wouldn't exist without the ad. Neither dashboard will sort it for you.

## The halo effect is real, and slow

The more generous theory, that people see an ad and return by name later, has a long history in search. Google's own [2011 research on paused search campaigns](https://research.google/pubs/incremental-clicks-impact-of-search-advertising/) found that most paid clicks were not replaced by organic clicks when ads stopped. Google, unsurprisingly, used that to argue for more ad spending. A few years later, [economists at eBay](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20171) found close to the opposite for branded keywords. Most people clicking an ad for "eBay" would have ended up on eBay anyway.

A decade of arguing over those studies left marketers with an unsatisfying conclusion. Halo effects and cannibalization both exist, they vary by category, and last-click analytics can't measure either. A delayed visit from someone who already knows your name, like that surprise deal in the CRM, looks like a halo. A same-day collapse in traffic doesn't.

## The ads could be changing the answers

Nobody can rule this out, and marketers have reasons to stay suspicious. OpenAI's ad business crossed a $1 billion annualized run rate in August, and [State of Brand reported](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/chatgpt-ads-paid-ai-answers) that it still fell well short of a $2.5 billion target for the year. Companies that are behind on ad revenue rarely respond by selling less.

The available data points the other way, though. Whitebox tracked more than 150,000 sponsored placements between April and August and [found that only 16.4%](https://thewhitebox.io/blog/openai-ads-market-report-2026) of the brands ChatGPT names in its answers had ever advertised on the platform. If ad spend bought organic mentions, the brands being named would mostly be the ones paying. They mostly aren't.

The research that could settle the question hasn't been done. As of late July, AI visibility company Geoptimizer [noted that no public study](https://www.geoptimizer.io/blog/chatgpt-ads-organic-ai-visibility) had compared organic citations in answers that carry ads against matched answers without them.

## Nobody can audit the answer

Google spent two decades fielding this accusation. Plenty of SEOs had a story about a client whose rankings improved after they started buying AdWords. Google denied it every time, and the suspicion never went away, because nobody outside Google could inspect the ranking system.

ChatGPT is harder to audit than Google ever was. A Google results page looks roughly the same for most people. A ChatGPT answer changes with the phrasing, the conversation history, saved memory and personalization. The ad slot rotates constantly on top of that. Whitebox found that asking the same question twice brought back a different advertiser [84.2% of the time](https://thewhitebox.io/blog/openai-ads-market-report-2026). Put an answer that shifts on every ask next to an ad that shifts on every ask, and a few weeks of data can support almost any theory.

Organic citations swing hard even without advertising in the picture. Reddit [lost 86% of its ChatGPT citations in four days](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/reddit-chatgpt-citations-platform-risk), and the listicles agencies built to win AI citations [lost half of them](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/chatgpt-google-listicle-citations-collapse). When the baseline moves that much on its own, lining up a traffic chart against an ad calendar proves very little.

Even if most of the reported lift turns out to be mislabeled ad clicks, the argument over it gives an early look at how organic AI visibility will be contested for years.

## Is this where AI search is headed?

If the pattern holds, a few things are likely.

Organic AI traffic will become one of the least trusted numbers in the marketing report. For two years it was the proof point for answer engine optimization, a line that kept going up. Now any team running ads without clean tagging has a contaminated series, and any CFO has a reason to ask whether the organic growth was paid for. That's a hard conversation for a discipline whose own measurement vendors are still [arguing over their margins of error](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/ai-visibility-measurement-margin-of-error), and marketers already struggle to [pitch brand spending to finance](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/cfo-brand-budget-investor-pitch) without it. Teams that can't separate the two streams will struggle to defend either one.

Paid and organic will keep taking credit for each other's results. The CRM deal shows how easily it happens. The ad dashboard showed nothing, and the CRM showed a major opportunity from organic ChatGPT. Depending on who presents it, that's proof the ads work or proof they don't. Without a holdout test, it proves neither.

Belief may shape budgets more than the facts do. If enough buyers decide that ads help organic presence, defensive spending turns into a cost of staying visible, the way bidding on your own brand name in Google became standard practice around 2010. OpenAI wouldn't need to change a single answer for that to happen. It would only need to remain impossible to verify. The market is already leaning that way. Some brands are [paying to get into AI answers](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/advertorial-takedown-restore-fees) through sponsored articles, and a sponsored card is [the only guaranteed slot](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/chatgpt-ads-paid-ai-answers) on the screen. The more likely future of AI search is one where paying to be found becomes normal simply because nobody can prove it isn't required.

What still can't be bought is a place inside the answer itself. The Whitebox data suggests most of the brands ChatGPT recommends got there without spending a dollar on ads. They got there through what other people publish about them, since [AI barely uses your own website](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/ai-search-third-party-citations-strategy) to describe your brand, and [most of what ChatGPT cites doesn't even rank on Google](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/great-flattening-ai-search-invisible-brands). The brands doing well have leaned on [Reddit and owned media rather than traditional PR](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/earned-media-ai-citations-reddit-owned-media), and more of them are [building publications of their own](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/what-is-owned-media-b2b). That part of AI visibility is still worth building, and it's also the part most likely to be undercounted when budgets get cut.

## What marketers can do now

Tag every ad URL. Add your own `utm_source` and `utm_medium` values to each ChatGPT ad destination, and set up a GA4 channel group that routes paid ChatGPT traffic ahead of the chatgpt.com referral bucket. [PaidSync's setup guide](https://paidsync.ai/blog/measure-chatgpt-ads-in-ga4) walks through the rules. If campaigns have run untagged, treat your organic AI trend line as unreliable from launch day on.

Audit past sessions. Filter historical organic ChatGPT visits for landing URLs that contain `oppref`. Each of those was an ad click. Compare landing pages too. A spike in organic traffic to the exact page your ads point to is a giveaway.

Run a holdout. Pause ads in one market or product line for three to four weeks while they keep running elsewhere, and track organic mention rates on a fixed set of prompts alongside traffic. If mentions hold steady while traffic falls, the traffic was coming from the ads.

Measure mentions apart from traffic. Logged-out or API-based prompt tracking never displays ads, so it shows whether the model names you without any chance of a missing UTM skewing the result.

Ask your buyers. For large deals, a self-reported "Where did you first hear about us?" field still does better than any dashboard at telling a halo apart from coincidence.

And if a team does all of that and still sees organic mentions rise and fall with ad spend, it should publish the data. That's the study the industry doesn't have yet.

Title: Clipping 101: Inside The Clipping Economy

URL Source: https://www.netinfluencer.com/clipping-101-inside-the-clipping-economy/

Published Time: 2026-09-26T16:22:59-04:00

Markdown Content:
### [Commentary](https://www.netinfluencer.com/commentary/)

![Image 1: Nii A. Ahene](https://www.netinfluencer.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/1532959354940-45x45.jpg)

Published on September 26, 2026

You have probably heard of the concept of clipping. You have definitely seen it. A podcast moment cut to thirty seconds and posted by an account with a generic name and no bio, or the same movie scene showing up from four different pages in one afternoon.

These short video clips have proliferated across every social media platform, from TikTok to Instagram to LinkedIn, blending into the fabric of the feed, with most watchers paying little attention to where the content came from or why it is there. But behind many of them is an ecosystem and an incentive model that produces these clips at scale for reach and engagement.

A brand posting to its own account gets one shot at the algorithm. A clipping network gets thousands, from thousands of accounts, and the brand only pays for the ones that land. Welcome to the world of clipping.

Companies from record labels to movie studios to streamers have already embraced the concept, leveraging their deep content catalogs to reach audiences that would never visit their own channels. We spoke with the founders of six clipping agencies to find out how the business works, where the money goes, and whether the model can be extended to the consumer brands that make up the core of the creator economy.

## The brand pays after, and only for views that clear a floor

> ![Image 2](blob:http://localhost/35362c1a91c9476cc06bd8ce47f93234)

A clipping campaign begins with a brief. The brand tells the agency which platforms it wants, who should be tagged, and what the clips can and cannot say. The agency turns that into a one-page requirement sheet for the clippers. The brand then sets two numbers: a total budget, and a rate for every thousand views a clip earns.

The brand decides how far the campaign reaches. Some are open to the agency’s entire network. Some require clippers to apply, and the brand approves each account. On longer contracts, agencies build pages for a single brand and staff them with clippers on retainer.

Then the campaign goes live. Thousands of clippers receive a notification. They download the footage, cut a clip, post it to their own page, and submit the link. Within a day, hundreds of versions of the same footage are in circulation, posted by people the brand has never met.

No one is paid until a post clears a threshold, typically somewhere between one thousand and ten thousand views depending on the agency. Every post that clears it is reviewed by a person. A post that violates the requirement sheet is rejected and never paid. When the budget is spent, the campaign ends. The brand receives a report. The clippers are paid.

Budgets are small by the standards of a media buy. Most campaigns run from a few thousand dollars to the low tens of thousands. How much of the budget reaches the clippers varies by agency, and the split is rarely shown to the client. The universal across all campaigns is that clipping is performance based. Brands only pay for views that were delivered and verified.

## From Meme Pages to Paid Placements

> ![Image 3](blob:http://localhost/d5d6ab41568958f062a4b568748908b9)

Most clippers started as fans running a page for free, a meme account, an athlete fan page, a celebrity news feed, and until recently the only way to earn from one was to message brands and ask for a promo fee. Clipping gives the same people, who already know what their corner of the internet will watch, a way to get paid for that instinct.

Nearly all of them do this on the side. The agency founders we spoke with describe high school students, college students, and parents with day jobs. Most run one or two pages. A small number run dozens.

The pages and accounts remain the property of the people who built them. Most earn little from them. A few earn a great deal. [Turan Selvi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/turan-selvi/) of [Clipster](https://www.netinfluencer.com/a-music-agency-campaign-management-problem-became-the-blueprint-for-a-creator-clipping-marketplace/) described one. “We had one creator that came to us that was posting movie edits for free, making hundreds of thousands of views, and he had no clue that there’s actually labels paying for it. He went from making nothing to making $9,000 in his first month. We have over 20 creators that make consistently over $10,000 per month, and on the very top end, the record month was $60,000.” He added a caveat. “The clippers that make the most money have pre-existing channels, networks, content that they already post. I don’t think clipping is a thing where someone just sits on their couch, sees an ad, downloads TikTok, creates an account, and suddenly they make $10,000 next month.”

## The few clips that work become the ad campaign

> ![Image 4](blob:http://localhost/c54b3a6c0c8f1306a65fbd757f720e02)

A brand that runs a clipping campaign gets two things back. The first is the views themselves, spread across pages the brand does not own. The count cannot show whether the people watching were new to the brand or had seen it four times already, because the platforms do not release that data. The founders’ case is that a brand is paid attention to by being seen repeatedly, and that clipping is bought for repetition as much as for reach.

The second is a creative test. Out of thousands of posts, a few dozen work, and those get run again as paid ads, from the brand’s own account or, through boost and partner codes, directly from the clipper’s page, where they perform because they do not read as ads. [Alec Schweitzer](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alec-schweitzer-990198103/) of [The Clip Ship](https://www.netinfluencer.com/the-clip-ship-alec-schweitzer-wants-brands-to-replace-bigger-ad-buys-with-thousands-of-organic-clips/) describes clipping as a test bed for paid creative, thousands of variations run for the price of the views, with the best few promoted, and calls the result “paid social 2.0,” then in the same breath “technically paid social.”

Amirzadeh, takes it a step further. Clip finds the clippers whose pages worked and hires them on retainer to run pages the brand owns. For the clipper it is an hour or two a day at a steady rate. For the brand it is an audience it gets to keep. Clip’s entertainment clients get one more thing. For the studios and production companies it clips shows for, Clip pulls the comments from every post and maps which scenes drew the most attention, because Netflix, Hulu, Peacock and Tubi do not share audience data with the studios whose shows they carry. A clipping campaign for a reality show doubles as the research the streamer will not provide.

## Much of what gets clipped belongs to someone else

> ![Image 5](blob:http://localhost/ff299e7adbaab2fc3846d0c19111faca)

All of this sits in a legal gray area. Clipping is built on reposting, and for every clipper working directly with a copyright owner there are probably ten more sideloading someone else’s footage onto the platforms: scenes from films and shows, moments from other people’s streams, songs nobody licensed.

[Evan Stanfield](https://www.linkedin.com/in/evan-stanfield-88709b297/) of [Clipping Culture](https://www.netinfluencer.com/college-dropout-builds-clipping-agency-driving-billions-of-views-for-brands-musicians/) calls it “a little bit of a gray area” and says it happens constantly. [Jake Cass](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jakecass93/) spent seventeen years in content identification before founding Empyre, which licenses a creator’s footage to fans under an agreement that binds them to platform rules, and he describes the unlicensed version as a ticking time bomb. Even when the brand supplies its own footage, who owns the clips afterward depends on the agency. [Lumina Clippers](https://www.netinfluencer.com/enterprise-clipping-agency-lumina-clippers-sells-distribution-to-the-brands-paid-social-wont-take/) writes full rights into its clipper terms, others leave it to the brand to define, and at some shops the question is never asked.

Apart from the copyright question, the view count itself has pitfalls. Views can be bought, from services that sell them outright and from clippers who know where to buy, and the agencies range from checking every post to checking nothing. Clipster says it has banned more than 20,000 creators for it. Even an honest count shows only a number. It cannot say who watched or whether they had seen the brand before, and on an open campaign the brand rarely learns which accounts posted.

The clips sit on pages nobody vetted, next to political content, gambling and adult material, and a clipper chasing views can turn to rage bait with the brand’s footage. Disclosure varies. Some agencies require an ad hashtag on every paid post, others leave it to the brief. Cass raises the case that worries him most: a regulated advertiser, a casino or an alcohol brand, that would face age and targeting rules on a platform’s own ad system, and instead pays clippers to put the same message into feeds the algorithm alone decides, including the feeds of minors and addicts.

## “We can’t turn shit into diamonds”

> ![Image 6](blob:http://localhost/79b6b38f39f54c3f689bc9f0d5351a07)

There is a reason clipping got its foothold with entertainment brands. It works best when people already want to watch the footage, when there is hours of it, and when the clip is itself the thing being sold, a song, a show, a stream, rather than something the clip has to point to. A podcast, a concert, a trailer all pass that test without trying. At Clip, [Nicolai Amirzadeh’s](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nicolai-amirzadeh/) team looks at the footage before it talks about anything else. “We look at the content first and see what their goals are,” he said. “Then we let them know, from our own view, is this content actually good enough to be amplified? Because we can’t turn shit into diamonds.” That is also what separates clipping from the tools a brand marketer already uses. UGC is a creator making something original about a product, usually on camera, for a flat fee. Whitelisting is a brand running ads from a creator’s own account. In clipping nobody makes anything new, so the footage decides everything.

The founders draw the hardest line around physical products. “I have yet to see anyone succeed with clipping for physical brands,” Selvi said. A product needs someone on camera holding it, and clippers do not show their faces, so those brands have stayed in UGC. The agencies that want their business say the fix is on the brand’s side. Alec Schweitzer of The Clip Ship sees the opening in “brands that are more open to testing and developing content from the ground up, and then distributing that with clipping.” The footage has to be worth watching before the product is in it.

Whether the model extends beyond entertainment, then, depends on brands making that footage, and on what they expect from it once they do. Rhys Mckay of Lumina Clippers is blunt about the second part. “It’s not affiliate marketing. Anyone who tells you that is lying. It’s not influencer marketing. Anyone who tells you that is lying. It’s awareness. It’s top of funnel.” Amirzadeh says clipping is already a line item in a few niches and becomes one elsewhere only when clients bring the agency into the wider marketing plan “instead of trying to fit clipping into this thing and think, nice.” The first buyers from outside entertainment have arrived. Mckay says the inbound in the last three months has come from large technology companies including a social media giant.

## Subscribe to Our Newsletter

  

## Check Out Our Podcast

![Image 7: Nii A. Ahene](blob:http://localhost/346dadc7249b4f18bcd4f1d0d397bce6)

[Nii A. Ahene](https://www.netinfluencer.com/author/nii/)

Nii A. Ahene is the founder and managing director of Net Influencer, a website dedicated to offering insights into the influencer marketing industry. Together with its newsletter, Influencer Weekly, Net Influencer provides news, commentary, and analysis of the events shaping the creator and influencer marketing space. Through interviews with startups, influencers, brands, and platforms, Nii and his team explore how influencer marketing is being effectively used to benefit businesses and personal brands alike.

![Image 8](https://netinfluencer.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/NetInfluencerPlan600px.png)
