Title: How to Use Customer Language for Powerful Marketing Copy

URL Source: https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing

Published Time: 2026-09-25T12:30:30+00:00

Markdown Content:
Most businesses describe themselves differently from how their customers do.

*   A roofing company talks about “comprehensive exterior restoration services.” Customers just search “roof leak after storm.”
*   A dentist promotes “comprehensive orthodontic solutions,” while the patient on the phone is asking how much Invisalign costs.
*   A marketing agency pitches “full-funnel demand generation.” The prospect just wants more leads.
*   And a car rental company leads with “premium fleet solutions” when the traveler on the other end really just wants to know if they can skip the deposit.

That gap shows up everywhere a business talks to a customer: in ads, on landing pages, in search results, in AI answers.

And the cost shows up in different places too.

Customers don’t recognize that you’re solving their problem, so conversion rates take the hit first. Ad costs creep up next, since Google’s [Quality Score](https://www.wordstream.com/quality-score) rewards ads that match what people actually typed. [SEO suffers because the business is chasing phrases nobody searches for](https://www.seo-theory.com/long-tail-content-strategy-for-people-who-dont-understand-the-long-tail/). And AI tools, which lean on the language people actually use when they talk about a product or service, have a harder time placing the business in an answer at all.

The businesses that consistently outperform their competitors tend to do one thing well: **They mirror the language customers already use**.

Here’s how to find that language, where it pays off first, and how to turn it into a habit instead of a one-time fix.

## Contents

*   [Why customer language matters more than ever](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing#why-customer-language-matters)
*   [The fastest way to find customer language](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing#fastest-way-find-customer-language)
*   [How to use customer language to improve your marketing copy](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing#how-to-use-customer-language)
*   [Common mistakes that keep businesses stuck](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing#common-customer-language-mistakes)
*   [A simple customer language audit](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing#customer-language-audit)
*   [Your customer language action plan](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/customer-language-in-marketing#customer-language-action-plan)

## Why customer language matters more than ever

**People rarely describe problems the way businesses describe solutions, and the distance between those two things has always cost businesses money. What’s changed is how much that distance costs now.**

For most of the last decade, a business could get away with formal, jargon-heavy copy as long as it ranked well and had a decent website. Customers would find the page, figure out what the business actually did, and convert anyway. That buffer is shrinking. Two things are driving it.

### 1. Search engines have gotten much better at understanding intent

[Google no longer just matches keywords to pages](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/prompt-based-keyword-research). It tries to understand what the person searching actually wants and surfaces content that delivers it clearly.

**Example**: A roofing company with a page titled “What to Do When Your Roof Is Leaking” will often outperform a competitor with a page titled “Residential Roofing Services,” even if the competitor has more [backlinks](https://www.wordstream.com/link-building), because one page is written in the language of the problem and the other is written in the language of the solution.

![Image 1: the results for this query use natural language to address the problem](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/leaking-roof-search.webp)

### 2. AI systems like Google’s AI Overviews and ChatGPT are trained on how people actually talk: reviews, forums, Reddit threads, support conversations, Q&A sites

That language becomes part of the retrieval layer that shapes what gets recommended. When a business writes exclusively in internal terminology, it’s optimizing for an audience that isn’t doing the searching.

[Stephanie Yoder](https://www.linkedin.com/in/stephanie-yoder/), Director of Content Strategy at [LaunchSquad](https://launchsquad.com/), puts it directly: “Most brands are still writing for keyword match. AI retrieval doesn’t work that way, and if your content doesn’t show up in that conversation, neither does your brand.”

**Example:** A pediatric dentist who writes about “anxiety-free pediatric oral care” is not speaking the same language as the parent typing “dentist good with scared kids” into Google at 11 p.m.

![Image 2: ai overview result for search for dentist for anxious kids](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ai-overview-result-dentist-for-anxious-kids.webp)

This matters even more because there’s less room than ever to make a second impression. [Zero-click searches](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/zero-click-searches), meaning **searches that end without a click to any website, reached roughly 68% in early 2026, up from about 60% in 2024 and under 50% a decade ago**, according to [SparkToro and Similarweb data](https://sparktoro.com/blog/in-2026-less-than-one-third-of-google-searches-still-send-a-click/).

If a searcher never clicks through, **the words inside the AI answer or the search snippet are often the only chance a business gets to be understood**. Getting those words right is no longer optional.

![Image 3: 🛠️](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f6e0.svg)**Get everything you need to know about showing up in AI search in our free guide:**[The AI Search Toolkit >>](https://www.wordstream.com/resources/ai-search-toolkit?cid=Web_WS_InContent_Guide_AISearchToolkit_Downloadd&itm_source=wordstream&itm_medium=blog&itm_campaign=incontent_links)

## The fastest way to find customer language

The good news is that most businesses are already sitting on the raw material. The research doesn’t require a budget or a tool subscription. **It requires paying attention to conversations that are already happening.**

### Start with your reviews

[Google reviews](https://localiq.com/blog/get-google-reviews/) are often the richest source of customer language because people writing them aren’t trying to sound professional. They’re just describing what happened and how it felt.

A plumbing company that reads through its last 50 Google reviews might find that a dozen of them say some version of “fixed it the same day.” That phrase is more valuable than anything the marketing team has written, because it captures exactly what anxious customers care about most when a pipe bursts. It belongs in a headline, not in paragraph four of a service page.

![Image 4: plumbing company review with customer language highlighted](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/plumbing-company-review-customer-language.webp)  
 A lawn care company in Phoenix might find five reviews that all mention some version of “finally someone who didn’t kill my grass in the summer heat.” That’s a targeting insight and a headline waiting to happen.

![Image 5: ⭐️](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/2b50.svg)**Get all the tips you need to collect more reviews in this free guide download >>**[How to Get More Reviews: 8 Tips to Boost Ranking, Reputation, & Revenue](https://www.wordstream.com/resources/how-to-get-more-reviews?cid=Web_WS_InContent_Guide_howtogetreviews_Download&itm_source=localiq&itm_medium=blog&itm_campaign=incontent_links)

### Ask customers what the AI said

Every other method in this section is about inferring customer language from behavior. This one is about getting it directly.

When a prospect mentions they found the business through ChatGPT or Perplexity, ask them to share the conversation. Some businesses are offering a small incentive, a $25 or $50 gift card, in exchange for a screenshot. It takes the customer one click.

What comes back is more useful than any [keyword tool](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/best-keyword-research-tools) or survey. The actual query they ran. The follow-up questions they asked inside the conversation. How the AI compared the business to competitors. What it said before the prospect ever picked up the phone.

![Image 6: chatgpt example prompt + business recommendation answer](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/chatgpt-query-vet-for-temperamental-dog.webp)

**One approach worth noting:** Many businesses have started doing this systematically with their sales teams, prompting the question any time a prospect mentions AI as a source. Within a few weeks, patterns emerge. Buyers aren’t searching “tell me about [business name].” They’re running deep comparison queries, asking about pricing, timelines, guarantees, and how the business stacks up against two or three specific competitors. In some cases, the AI is surfacing objections the sales team had never heard out loud.

No GEO tool replicates this. The synthetic prompts those tools generate are educated guesses about what customers might ask. This is the actual question, from a real person, in the moment they were deciding.

For a small business, even five or six of these conversations can reshape how the website is written, what the FAQ section covers, and which objections get addressed upfront.

### Read your support tickets and emails

Support teams hear real customer language every single day, and almost no one on the marketing side pays attention to it. The questions that come in again and again, the words customers use to describe frustration, the things they say they were confused about before they called: All of it is free research.

If every third support email from a dental practice’s patients asks some version of “does this hurt?” that fear deserves an answer on the website, not just on the phone.

### Listen to sales calls

[Recorded sales calls](https://localiq.com/products/ai-lead-management/) are one of the most underused content research tools available to small businesses. Prospects say exactly what they’re worried about, what they’ve already tried, how they’d describe success, and what would make them walk away.

![Image 7](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/dash-ai-lead-actions.png)

A roofing contractor whose sales team hears “I just want to know the price upfront; the last company wasted my time” has just been handed a headline: “Free Estimate in 24 Hours. No Pressure, No Surprises.”

### Pull your Google Ads search query report

If the business is running paid search, the [Search Terms report](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/google-ads-reports) shows the exact phrases people typed before they clicked on an ad. Most advertisers only open it to find negative keywords. That’s leaving money on the table. Read it as a transcript of customer language.

![Image 8: google ads tests - search terms](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/google-ads-tests-search-terms.webp)

An auto shop that sees “how much does a brake job cost” appearing 80 times a month now knows exactly what to put on its [landing page headline](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/landing-page-copywriting) and what to bid on more aggressively.

![Image 9: 🛑](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f6d1.svg)**Want to know how your Google Ads campaigns are doing _right now_?** Find out with a free, instant audit >>[Google Ads Performance Grader](https://www.wordstream.com/google-adwords?cid=Web_Any_InContentTextLink_PPC_AWGrader_AWGrader)

### Explore reddit, forums, and local community groups

Customers talk differently when no one is trying to sell them anything.

A thread in a local Facebook group asking “anyone know a good HVAC company that doesn’t overcharge?” will tell you more about what matters to that customer base than any survey could.

These conversations reveal the real buying triggers, the real objections, and the specific phrases that come up when people are just talking to their neighbors.

Let’s explore some of the ways you can use customer language to:

*   Cut ad costs
*   Improve conversion rates
*   Boost SEO
*   Increase AI visibility

### How to use customer language to cut your ad costs

Most customer-language advice focuses on branding and SEO. The fastest financial payoff is usually in paid search, and it works through a mechanism most small businesses don’t fully understand.

Google uses a [Quality Score](https://www.wordstream.com/quality-score) to evaluate how relevant an ad is to both the search query and the landing page it leads to. According to Google’s own Ads documentation, Quality Score is [direct input into Ad Rank and the cost-per-click an advertiser pays for a given position](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6167118?hl=en). A higher score can mean paying less for the same placement than a competitor with a lower one.

The language gap sits right at the center of that equation. Consider two auto repair shops bidding on the keyword “brake repair near me.” The first runs an ad that says “Professional Automotive Maintenance Services – ASE Certified Technicians.” The second runs an ad that says “Brake Repair Today – Most Jobs Done in Under 2 Hours.”

Both are targeting the same keyword, bidding similar amounts, and appearing in the same auction. But the second ad speaks the language of the search. It matches what the person typed and answers the unspoken question underneath it: how long is this going to take? That relevance earns a better Quality Score, which translates directly into a [lower cost per click](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/how-to-lower-cost-per-click).

![Image 10: brake repair query sponsored results using customer language](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/brake-repair-query-sponsored-results.webp)

### How to use customer language to improve conversion rates

Getting someone to click is only half the problem. What happens after the click depends almost entirely on whether the page they land on sounds like the answer they were looking for.

The highest-leverage place to apply customer language is in headlines, because that’s the first thing a visitor reads and the fastest way to signal that they’re in the right place. “Comprehensive Plumbing Solutions” tells a visitor nothing specific. “Need an Emergency Plumber? We’ll Be There Today” answers the question they had when they searched.

The closer the headline is to the customer’s actual words, the less work they have to do to decide whether to keep reading.

![Image 11: plumber ad using customer language](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/leaking-pipe-sponsored-results-customer-language.webp)

Service pages are where the language gap tends to do the most quiet damage. A page called “Our Services” is a menu. A page called “How Much Does Emergency Plumbing Cost in Chicago?” is an answer to a real question a real person typed. The second approach doesn’t just [improve SEO](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/local-seo-tips). It also signals to the visitor that this business understands their situation, which builds enough trust to keep them on the page.

[Calls to action](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/call-to-action-examples) follow the same pattern. “Contact Us” is a direction. “Get a Free Roof Inspection” is an offer. “See 3 Ways to Get More Leads This Month” is a promise tied to the exact outcome the prospect cares about. Small agencies that have tested variations of these consistently find that the more specific and customer-centric the [CTA](https://www.wordstream.com/cta-generator), the higher the conversion rate, because the customer can see exactly what they’re getting before they click.

The underlying principle is straightforward: the closer the language on the page is to the language in the customer’s head, the less friction stands between them and a decision.

![Image 12: 🚀](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f680.svg)**Ready to quickly increase your conversions and win more customers?** Download our guide: [Super-Fast Ways to Boost Conversions >>](https://www.wordstream.com/resources/ways-to-boost-conversions?cid=Web_WS_InContent_Guide_BoostConversionRates_Download&itm_source=wordstream&itm_medium=blog&itm_campaign=incontent_links)

### How to use customer language to improve SEO

Most businesses do [keyword research](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/how-to-do-keyword-research) backward. They start with a tool, find terms with decent search volume, and write content around those terms. The problem is that keyword tools surface what people search, not necessarily how they phrase the actual question. Customer language research fills that gap.

A dental practice doing standard keyword research might target “orthodontic treatment options.” A practice that’s been reading its reviews and listening to consultations knows that patients are actually searching “braces vs. Invisalign cost” and “does Invisalign hurt more than braces.” Those [long-tail, conversational queries](https://www.wordstream.com/long-tail-keywords) are often less competitive, more specific to buying intent, and far more aligned with what the practice’s prospective patients are actually thinking about.

![Image 13: invisalign vs braces google search with customer language in search results](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/invisalign-vs-braces-google-search-results.webp)

The same applies to content topics. Customer questions are content briefs in disguise. An HVAC company whose service team hears “should I repair my AC or just replace it?” three times a week has an article topic that is already validated by demand. A property management company whose inbox fills up every spring with “how do I get my security deposit back?” has a piece that will rank for a phrase thousands of people search every year.

None of this requires a content strategist. It requires listening to what customers are already asking and then writing the clearest possible answer.

### How to use customer language to improve AI visibility

[AI search](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ai-search-signals) doesn’t work the way keyword-based search does, and that changes what good optimization looks like.

When someone types a question into ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google’s AI Overviews, they’re usually asking the way they’d ask a person. “Who’s the best pediatric dentist in Tampa for anxious kids?” “What should I do when my furnace stops working in the middle of winter?” “Is it worth getting a home warranty?” These are conversational queries, not keyword strings.

**Content that’s written in that same conversational register is easier for AI systems to retrieve and surface as an answer, because it maps more naturally onto the question being asked.**

![Image 14: chatgpt results dentist for anxious kids tampa ](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/chatgpt-results-dentist-for-anxious-kids-tampa.webp)

Reviews play a larger role in AI visibility than most businesses realize. AI systems don’t just index formal website content. They synthesize information from across the web, and reviews are part of that picture.

A review that says “They fixed our furnace the same day we called, right before a cold snap, and the technician explained exactly what went wrong” is useful to an AI system trying to answer “who’s a reliable HVAC company in [city]?”

A review that just says “great service, highly recommend” is not. [Encouraging customers to write specific, detailed reviews](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/how-to-ask-for-reviews) is one of the most underused tactics for improving how a business shows up in AI-generated answers.

## Common mistakes that keep businesses stuck

Understanding why businesses default to jargon makes it easier to stop doing it. Most of the time, it isn’t carelessness. It’s that the people writing the copy are too close to the product.

Writing for peers instead of customers is the most common pattern. Industry language sounds competent inside a business. It signals expertise to colleagues, impresses people at trade shows, and feels appropriate on a website that’s meant to represent a professional organization. The problem is that customers are not the business’s peers. A homeowner dealing with a burst pipe at midnight doesn’t want to evaluate credentials. She wants to know someone will show up.

Hiding simple answers behind complexity is related but slightly different. Some businesses bury the most useful information, prices, timelines, process, exactly what’s included, deep in their pages out of habit or a misguided sense that giving too much away loses the sale. In practice, the opposite is usually true.

A roofing company that puts “most residential roof replacements cost between $8,000 and $15,000 depending on size and material, and we’ll give you an exact quote within 24 hours” on its homepage will convert better than one that says “contact us for a personalized estimate,” because it answers the question before the customer has to ask.

![Image 15: roof replacement cost content example](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/roof-replacement-cost-content-example.webp)

As Stephanie puts it: “The instinct to withhold pricing usually backfires. By the time a customer has to call to ask, half of them have already moved on.”

## A simple customer language audit

Before running a full strategy overhaul, it’s worth doing a quick diagnostic on what’s already live. Open the homepage, a core service page, the best-performing blog post, and if the business runs paid search, the Google Ads search query report from the last 30 days.

Read through each one and ask a single question: **Could I find these exact phrases in a customer review, a support email, or a sales call transcript?**

If the answer is mostly no, there’s a gap. The audit doesn’t need to be exhaustive to be useful. Even identifying two or three places where the business is speaking past its customers is enough to get started.

## Your customer language action plan

The goal here isn’t to rewrite everything at once. That’s how these projects stall. The goal is to make one targeted change, measure it, and build the habit from there.

**This week, pull the raw material:** 15 to 20 recent reviews, last month’s support tickets, and if the business advertises, the search query report from Google Ads. Read through all of it and tag every phrase that repeats more than twice. Those repeating phrases are the signal. They’re the things customers care about enough to keep saying in their own words.

**Then rewrite three things, not the whole site.** Pick one [headline](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/headline-formulas), one CTA, and one ad headline if applicable. Swap in the customer’s exact phrasing and leave everything else alone for now. Changing only three things makes the impact measurable. If the conversion rate on the service page goes up and the CPC on the ad goes down, you know the language change is doing something.

**Check the numbers in 30 days, then make it a quarterly habit.** Customer language isn’t static. New reviews come in, new search terms emerge, and the phrases that resonated last year start to drift. Businesses that treat this as ongoing research rather than a one-time project end up with marketing that stays aligned with how customers actually talk, which is the only way to make sure it keeps working.

kept.blurb: Test trial length based on how quickly users experience value, how often they need to return, and the cost of free access. Title: How long should your free trial be? Data from 17,000+ apps

URL Source: https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/free-trial-length

Published Time: 2026-09-28T09:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Free trials keep dividing app developers. Give users more time, get paid faster, or skip the trial entirely?

Sure, shorter trials mean earlier payments, faster feedback for paid campaigns, and lower costs of providing free access. That last one matters most if you’re running an AI app, where every free session carries a real, variable cost behind it.

Yet our State of Subscription Apps 2026 report found a 42.5% median conversion rate for trials of 17+ days, versus 25.5% for trials of four days or less. That’s roughly 67% higher.

But do those subscribers keep paying? And does the pattern differ depending on subscription plans?

We analyzed 17,000+ apps to benchmark conversion and renewal across trial durations for weekly, monthly, and annual subscriptions. We also compared AI and non-AI apps and explored differences by category and subscriber region.

## Which trial lengths do high-volume apps choose?

First things first: we looked at the 100 apps with the most trial starts in each category and plan duration, and checked what trial length each one runs.

Short trials tend to dominate. On weekly plans, 81–100 of those apps use trials of four days or less, depending on category.

![Image 1: Weekly subscription trial lengths among each category’s top 100 apps. Trials of four days or less dominate every category, ranging from 81% in Health & Fitness to 100% in Gaming.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/b95c2ef046ff518c583822d025e68a5a2bc879b8-3842x2800.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

Monthly and annual plans also lean toward trials of nine days or less, although the mix varies by category.

Education, Health & Fitness, and Travel favor 5–9-day trials, while Productivity and Photo & Video favor trials of four days or less. One possible explanation is how long users need to evaluate the app: some benefits take repeated use to assess, while others are apparent in a single session.

![Image 2: Trial length distribution among each category’s top 100 apps for monthly and annual subscriptions. Trials of 5–9 days lead in most categories, while trials of four days or less are most common in Gaming and Photo & Video.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/a8b07bcffee52aba8602b501cbe55dc661dcbccf-1921x2400.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

These are apps with the most trial starts, rather than the highest revenue or retention. Their choices show what’s common at scale. But this doesn’t establish which trial length _performs_ best.

That leaves a useful question: how do conversion and renewal compare across those common short trials? And what changes in the less common, longer-trial groups?

## How many trial users reach a second payment?

Our data actually shows that longer trials are often associated with higher renewal rates, though the pattern varies by subscription plan:

*   **Weekly subscriptions:** The share of trial users who paid and renewed once is slightly higher after 5–9-day trials than after trials of four days or less: **14.4% vs. 11.8%**. Evidence for longer trials remains limited.
*   **Monthly subscriptions:** Longer trials are associated with more trial users paying and renewing: **30.6%** after 10–16-day trials vs. **18.5%**after trials of four days or less. The pattern then levels off in the 17–32-day trial group.
*   **Annual subscriptions:** The share of trial users who paid and renewed increases with trial length across all four groups, from **3.5%** after trials of four days or less to**18.5%**after 17–32-day trials. Though trial duration alone may not explain higher retention.

![Image 3: Share of trials that convert to paid subscriptions and renew once, by plan and trial length. Monthly plans rise from 18% to around 30%, and annual plans from 3% to 18%. Weekly estimates for trials longer than nine days are based on fewer than 20 apps.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/17cf835cbccd288d0ddc8c22c2199f75148050a8-1921x1080.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

_One caveat before we go further: there is a correlational pattern, and a flattering one. Someone who’s still in your trial on day 25 of a 30-day window is simply more likely to pay than someone who bails on day two. Keep that in mind as the ceilings and floors get more specific below._

## Do conversion and renewal favor the same trial length?

We also looked at conversion and first renewal separately to see whether longer trials coincide with more users paying, more paying subscribers renewing, or both.

For**weekly** subscriptions, the difference between the two common short-trial groups is larger at renewal. Trials of 5–9 days convert 24.3% of trial users, compared with 22.3% for trials of four days or less. Among paying subscribers, 65.9% renew after 5–9-day trials, versus 57.9% after shorter trials.

There are too few qualifying apps offering weekly plans with trials beyond nine days to extend that comparison reliably.

![Image 4: Weekly subscription trial conversion and first renewal rates by trial length. Conversion is 22% for trials of four days or less and 24% for 5–9 days; first renewal among paying subscribers is 58% and 66%, respectively.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/cb69c0787ba3a034c60784232fe3117dda4980b4-1921x1080.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

For**monthly** subscriptions, conversion is higher in the 5–9-day trial group than in the shortest-trial group: 45.9% versus 39.6%. The 10–16-day group has similar conversion, at 46.6%, but higher first renewal: 72.0% versus 62.8% of paying subscribers.

The 17–32-day group has the highest first renewal rate, at 77.5%, but lower conversion than either middle group, at 43.7%.

![Image 5: Monthly subscription trial conversion and first renewal rates by trial length. Conversion is 40%, 46%, 47%, and 44% for trials of four days or less, 5–9, 10–16, and 17–32 days, respectively.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/b0aafb8914b89db29588a7d5e78cd7f054b1a227-1921x1080.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

For **annual** subscriptions, both rates are higher across longer-trial groups. Comparing trials of four days or less with 17–32-day trials, conversion rise from 24% to 44.6%, and first renewal from 18.3% to 47.5%.

Of course, a trial rarely builds a year of loyalty on its own: a longer trial mostly gives annual buyers more time to be sure before a bigger, harder-to-reverse commitment. So the people who convert after that longer look might already be the ones less likely to cancel.

![Image 6: Annual subscription trial conversion and first renewal rates by trial length. Conversion is 24%, 33%, 43%, and 45% for trials of four days or less, 5–9, 10–16, and 17–32 days, respectively.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/2f2620df57e66936da0b2d994fa4845d79618764-1921x1080.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

## What if you remove the trial altogether?

Here’s another interesting finding: subscriptions purchased without a trial have lower first-renewal rates on weekly and monthly plans than those that begin with one.

The weekly gap is particularly large: 35.9% of paying subscribers renew without a trial, compared with 57.9% after trials of four days or less and 65.9% after 5–9-day trials.

Annual plans show a different pattern. No-trial renewal is higher than renewal after trials of up to nine days, but lower than after longer trials.

| **Trial length** | **Weekly (1st renewal)** | **Monthly (1st renewal)** | **Annual (1st renewal)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No trial | 35.9% | 49.5% | 26.6% |
| Trial of four days or less | 57.9% | 54.2% | 18.3% |
| Trial of 5–9 days | 65.9% | 62.8% | 25.3% |
| Trial of 10–16 days | Too few apps | 72% | 36.4% |
| Trial of 17–32 days | Too few apps | 77.5% | 47.5% |

_Note: this table measures first renewal among paying subscribers, not all trial users, so these numbers run higher. This comparison a;sp doesn’t tell us how many people purchase when shown a no-trial offer._

Lower renewal doesn’t automatically make a no-trial offer less profitable, though. [David Vargas’s case study](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/should-your-app-stop-offering-free-trials) found that removing the trial, alongside changes to pricing and plans, helped one app earn enough per paying customer to support paid acquisition without it.

## How does trial length relate to conversion and renewal in AI apps?

For AI apps with usage-based inference or generation costs, extra free access needs to justify its expense. Besides, [higher churn](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/ai-app-retention-study) with lower conversions means there's less room to get the length wrong.

The **monthly** results offer a useful comparison.

Trials of 5–9 days and 10–16 days show almost identical conversion, at 38.2% and 38.5%. First renewal is higher in the 10–16-day group, at 64.2% versus 57.4%.

But the 17–32-day group shows no further renewal gain: first renewal is 64.1%, while conversion falls to 31.8%. In this dataset, the longest monthly trials don’t provide a stronger conversion or renewal benchmark than 10–16-day trials.

![Image 7: For monthly subscriptions, AI apps have lower trial conversion and first renewal rates than non-AI apps at every trial length. Beyond 16 days, AI trial conversion falls from 39% to 32%, while first renewal stays at 64%.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/2b8f108620e9e08eb0571774cafdb4dab29ddc3f-1921x1800.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

For **annual AI subscriptions**, conversion is 33.8% after 10–16-day trials, compared with 23.3% after 5–9-day trials. First renewal is also higher, at 29.4% versus 19.6%. For **weekly AI subscriptions**, the difference is smaller. Conversion is 23.1% after 5–9-day trials versus 22.3% after trials of four days or less; first renewal is 62.5% versus 57.9%.

Without a trial, first renewal is lower on weekly and monthly AI plans. Annual no-trial renewal is 18.9%, compared with 15.1% after trials of four days or less and 19.6% after 5–9-day trials.

![Image 8: First renewal rates for AI subscriptions by trial duration and plan. Weekly rates rise from 33.8% without a trial to 62.5% with 5–9-day trials. Monthly rates rise from 41.3% without a trial to around 64% with 10–32-day trials. Annual rates range from 15.1% to 29.4%.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/27ccd923b1205b3e7ed58467fffa32a972b71240-3842x2160.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

## Does giving users more trial time improve conversion across regions?

On **annual** plans, North America and Western Europe have higher conversion across progressively longer-trial groups. Asia-Pacific follows that pattern up to 10–16 days, but has lower conversion in the 17–32-day group.

![Image 9: Annual subscription trial conversion by trial length across seven regions. Conversion rises through 10–16 days in every region. At 17–32 days, it increases further in North America, Western Europe, and Latin America but declines elsewhere. North America has the highest rates; India & Southeast Asia has the lowest.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/285979b02bcfc31113442b6f62ecef3f718aa4c6-1921x1080.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

On **monthly plans**, conversion in Middle East and Africa, India and Southeast Asia, and Latin America is highest in the 5–9-day group and lower in the 17–32-day group. The largest gap among these regions is in Middle East and Africa: 38.3% versus 27.4%.

![Image 10: Monthly subscription trial conversion by trial length across seven regions. North America and Asia-Pacific have the highest rates, while India & Southeast Asia has the lowest.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/52a2bea226f311b9b509e7dbfa3567d774991874-1921x1080.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

## Do the same trial lengths outperform across app categories?

On monthly plans, longer-trial groups generally have higher renewal rates across app categories.

But they don’t always have higher conversion. In many categories, conversion is highest in the 10–16-day group and lower in the 17–32-day group.

When interpreting these differences, consider two timelines: how quickly users recognize the app’s value, and how often they have a reason to return. The data don’t measure habit formation, but those questions can help you decide what extra trial days should accomplish.

![Image 11: Heatmap of monthly subscription trial conversion and first renewal rates across 11 app categories and four trial lengths. Conversion patterns vary by category, while longer trials generally have higher first renewal rates among paying subscribers. Dashed borders mark results based on fewer than 20 apps.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/c3qnx9b0/production/b726329a5c624396c25e04b83cefb11bb604d829-1921x1500.png?w=3840&q=100&auto=format&fit=max&sharp=15)

Three categories illustrate the differences:

*   **Media & Entertainment**: The 10–16-day group leads on both conversion (58.9%) and first renewal (79.4%), with neither rate higher in the 17–32-day group. For streaming apps, the question to explore is whether extra trial days help users discover more content they want to keep watching.
*   **Utilities**: Conversion is highest in the 10–16-day group, at 47.4%, compared with 44.0% in the 17–32-day group. First renewal is highest in the longest group, at 77.9%, versus 55% for trials of four days or less. A user might recognize a tool’s value after one task. The question for a longer trial is whether it gives them opportunities to use it again.
*   **Health & Fitness**: Conversion is higher in the 5–9-day group than in the 10–16-day group: 46.8% versus 40.4%. First renewal is higher across longer-trial groups, from 51.5% for trials of four days or less to 77.1% for 17–32-day trials. If you’re considering more trial time, check whether users keep completing workouts or logging progress during those extra days. That would give you evidence of continued engagement, rather than assuming a longer trial builds a habit.

## So, what's the right trial length for your app?

These findings make a case for challenging a short trial chosen by default. But they also show where longer trials have no clear advantage, helping you narrow down which alternatives deserve a test.

At the end of the day, the answer isn't "run longer (or shorter) trials," "cut trials entirely," or a number copied from the leader in your niche. It's whichever pattern matches your app:

*   **Time to value**. How long a user needs to experience your app before they can fairly judge whether it's worth paying for.
*   **Habit versus motivation**. Utilities' renewal kept climbing long after conversion had already peaked, because deciding fast and building a routine aren't the same thing. Health & Fitness runs the same tension the other way: a longer trial builds the habit, but it also gives motivation more time to fade first.
*   **Audience context**. Price sensitivity and trust in recurring billing can change what a longer trial buys: more confidence to pay, or just more time to back out. So does whether users are weighing you against a free alternative, and how much they need to learn before they can fairly judge your app at all.
*   **Cost**. Longer trial delays revenue and stretches out how long paid acquisition takes to pay for itself. If your app has a real per-user cost behind every session, that spend adds up whether or not the person converts.

The best next action? Use the benchmarks above as a starting point, then test trial length against your own subscription plans, your app's specifics, and what you know about your audience.

[RevenueCat Experiments](https://www.revenuecat.com/feature/experiments) lets you get there faster. Set trial length as the variable, and let your own revenue numbers make the call.

## How we analyzed the data

We compared trial conversion and paid renewal separately for weekly, monthly, and annual subscriptions on the App Store and Google Play, with breakdowns by platform, AI classification, category, and subscriber region. We also looked at the 100 apps with the most trial starts in each category.

*   **Period:** August 2025–July 2026, based on trial starts for conversion and renewal dates for retention. The combined trial-to-first-renewal measure follows the same trials through both payments, including earlier annual cohorts.
*   **Measurement:** Median app-level rates. Each renewal rate measures subscriptions that paid again, conditional on the previous payment.
*   **Sample requirements:** More than 100 eligible trials or subscriptions reaching first renewal per qualifying app segment. Groups with fewer than 20 apps are directional.
*   **Trial coverage:** No-trial subscriptions appear only in renewal comparisons. Trials longer than 32 days are excluded from conversion figures.

Title: Amazon will let sellers manage Walmart, eBay, Shopify and TikTok sales from their Amazon dashboards

URL Source: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/amazon-will-let-sellers-manage-walmart-ebay-shopify-and-tiktok-sales-from-their-amazon-dashboards/

Published Time: 2026-09-24T14:00:35+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1](https://cdn.geekwire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/mary-beth-2026.jpg)

Mary Beth Westmoreland, Amazon’s VP of Worldwide Selling Partner Experience, speaks Tuesday morning at Amazon Accelerate at the Seattle Convention Center. (GeekWire Photo / Todd Bishop) 

Amazon is [introducing](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/small-business/amazon-seller-central-multichannel-selling-tools) tools to let independent sellers manage their sales on four of its biggest rivals — eBay, Shopify, TikTok and, yes, even Walmart — from Seller Central, the same dashboard they use to run their Amazon businesses.

The multichannel selling tools, announced Thursday at Amazon’s Accelerate seller conference in Seattle, are rolling out gradually to U.S. sellers over the coming months at no extra cost. At first, sellers can connect their accounts on the other platforms, import and link listings, see all their orders in one place, and fulfill orders across channels.

**The data question:** The move raises natural questions about Amazon’s motives, including what the company might do with data from sellers’ businesses on rival platforms. In an interview, [Mary Beth Westmoreland](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marybethwestmoreland/), Amazon’s VP of Worldwide Selling Partner Experience, brought the issue up unprompted.

“A seller’s multichannel data that might surface in Seller Central, it’s never used for anything other than surfacing it to that specific seller. Period,” she said. “We never use that data for any other purpose.”

Pressed on whether the data could affect a seller’s standing on Amazon, such as by pushing their products lower in search results for charging less elsewhere, she was more emphatic. “We never, ever, will touch this data or use it for any other reason other than to show it to you,” she said.

Questions about how Amazon could use seller data for other purposes are not hypothetical. In 2020, The Wall Street Journal [reported](https://www.geekwire.com/2020/amazon-reportedly-used-third-party-seller-data-research-launch-products/) that Amazon employees had used data about independent sellers to develop competing house-brand products, and in 2022 Amazon agreed with [European regulators](https://www.geekwire.com/2022/how-amazon-is-changing-the-buy-box-in-europe-to-resolve-antitrust-concerns/) not to use sellers’ non-public data in its own retail business.

Amazon said at the time that it prohibits employees from using non-public, seller-specific data to decide which house-brand products to launch. When it settled with European regulators, the company said it still disagreed with “several of the preliminary conclusions” in the case.

The Federal Trade Commission’s pending [antitrust case](https://www.geekwire.com/2023/ftc-and-17-states-sue-amazon-for-maintaining-alleged-monopoly-power-that-stifles-competition/) also accuses Amazon of punishing sellers who offer lower prices on other sites, an allegation Amazon denies. The case is set for trial in March 2027.

**Why, then, is Amazon doing this?** Westmoreland said sellers told Amazon that managing sales across so many platforms takes too much time. “They said we would love it if we could use some of the cool tools in Seller Central everywhere we sell, and so that’s what we did,” she said.

In addition, she said, the company believes sellers who succeed on other platforms will bring a wider range of products to Amazon, which makes its store more appealing to shoppers, so helping sellers elsewhere ultimately benefits Amazon, too. More than 95% of Amazon’s independent sellers already sell through multiple channels, according to the company.

**What Amazon already offers:** The new multichannel tools in the Seller Central dashboard add to a collection of services Amazon already offers to merchants who sell elsewhere, potentially boosting its other services.

*   [Multi-Channel Fulfillment](https://sell.amazon.com/fulfillment-by-amazon/fba-multichannel), a paid service, ships orders from other sites out of Amazon’s warehouses, and last year [added integrations](https://www.geekwire.com/2025/sold-on-walmart-sent-by-amazon-the-weird-new-world-of-online-retail/) with Walmart, Shopify and SHEIN.
*   Amazon [Warehousing and Distribution](https://sell.amazon.com/programs/warehousing) stores inventory in bulk and restocks those warehouses and other channels.
*   [Buy with Prime](https://buywithprime.amazon.com/) lets merchants offer Prime delivery on their own websites, with Amazon handling customer service and returns.

Amazon also [announced](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/retail/amazon-mcf-prime-delivery-merchant-websites) Thursday that merchants using Multi-Channel Fulfillment in the U.S. can now offer Prime delivery on their own websites at no additional cost. It launched a separate pricing program that it says can cut their fulfillment fees by 15% to 25% for the first six months.

Selling services to merchants is a big business for Amazon. Independent sellers account for more than 60% of units sold on Amazon worldwide, and the fees Amazon charges them brought in $46.8 billion in the second quarter, more revenue than AWS.

**How it works:** Sellers connect their other accounts through a multichannel settings page in Seller Central. The Manage Orders page then shows unshipped orders from every connected channel on one screen. A seller can select a Shopify order, for example, and send it to Amazon for fulfillment, with tracking updates flowing back to Shopify automatically, according to Amazon.

Westmoreland said the connections to other platforms mostly use their standard APIs, along with existing agreements through Veeqo, the multichannel shipping software company Amazon [acquired in 2021](https://www.geekwire.com/2022/amazon-quietly-buys-another-multichannel-retail-technology-company-uk-based-veeqo/) and [now offers free](https://press.aboutamazon.com/2022/9/amazon-launches-veeqo-free-shipping-software-for-sellers-including-discounted-shipping-rates) to sellers. Sellers don’t have to use Amazon’s fulfillment services to use the new tools, she said.

Amazon says more features are coming, including the ability to edit a product description once and have it update on every channel, AI-generated listings for other platforms, and a dashboard showing how much sellers earn on each product across channels, including ad spend and traffic data from the other platforms.

**The competition:** The new tools also put Amazon in competition with companies that already sell multichannel software, including [Rithum](https://www.rithum.com/), formed from the combination of ChannelAdvisor, CommerceHub and Dsco, and [Linnworks](https://www.linnworks.com/).

Shopify offers its own version, [Marketplace Connect](https://apps.shopify.com/marketplace-connect), which lets merchants manage their Amazon, Walmart, eBay and Target Plus sales from inside Shopify — essentially the reverse of what Amazon is now offering.

Westmoreland called Amazon’s tools “one more option” for sellers. She also said sellers had told the company they were already paying for this kind of software: “Hey, I’m paying for it, and it’s hard to do. Can you do this for me?”

kept.heading: HOW X'S RANKING ALGORITHM WORKS (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: X's ranking algorithm favors posts that people are likely to share, reply to, or quote rather than simply like. A copy link share carries 40X the weight of a like, while replies and quotes each carry 10X the weight. Posts also need to stay focused on a clear topic to reach relevant nonfollowers, and negative actions such as mutes and reports carry heavy penalties. The algorithm also reduces the value of repeated posts from the same author and stops considering posts after 48 hours. Posting less often and creating highly shareable content can improve reach.

Title: How X's ranking algorithm works

URL Source: https://johnjwang.com/post/2026/09/25/how-xs-ranking-algorithm-works

Published Time: 2026-09-25T00:00:00Z

Markdown Content:
There’s a ton of folk wisdom on X about how to go viral. A few examples you’ll see over and over:

*   **Put links in the first reply instead of the post.** " ([Sprout Social](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/twitter-algorithm/)).
*   **Replies are king.** “A reply on your tweet is worth 13.5x a like,” and if you reply back, “a two-way conversation [is] worth 150x more than a single like” ([OpenTweet](https://opentweet.io/blog/x-algorithm-secrets-2026)).
*   **Pay for Premium.** Premium gets “roughly 4x for in-network reach to your own followers and about 2x for out-of-network reach to non-followers” ([SocialRails](https://socialrails.com/blog/how-to-grow-on-twitter-x-complete-guide)).

But it’s very hard to tell what’s real, and most of it traces back to code Twitter released in 2023. But X now publishes the production code for its “For You” feed at [xai-org/x-algorithm](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm) (including the ranking weights!) and they update it about every four weeks.

## How the ranker works

The basic trick of the ranking algorithm is to use something cheap to narrow the available options, then save the expensive model for a few thousand posts.

![Image 1: How X's ranker works. Index: Grok and Gemma LLMs read the post and preprocess it, and it becomes a six-number semantic ID. Retrieve: filter down from about 10 million posts to about 2,800, the nearest to your history and interests plus posts from people you follow. Rank: the Phoenix transformer scores each post by its predicted actions, as the sum of weight times the probability of about 25 actions.](https://johnjwang.com/images/x-pipeline.svg)

Source: [xai-org/x-algorithm](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm), September 2026 release.

1.   **Retrieval narrows ~10 million posts to ~2,800.** Most come from people you follow or from an embedding search for posts close to your recent history.
2.   **A transformer predicts what you’ll do.** Phoenix (whose code started as a port of Grok-1) reads your last ~1,000 actions and predicts the odds you’ll like, reply, share, mute, or report each post.
3.   **A weighted sum becomes the score.** Posts from people you don’t follow get multiplied by 0.75, and each extra post from the same author counts for less.

A few implementation details I found fascinating:

*   **The ranker never reads your words.** Its inputs are post IDs, author IDs, and actions. Your text only gets in through a _semantic ID_ (basically think of it like a small embedding): six numbers from 0 to 255. The first number picks one of 256 broad neighborhoods, and each number after that narrows it down further. Posts on the same topic end up sharing the first few numbers.
*   **An LLM also writes a report on every post.** A Gemma-based initial filter (called, hilariously, the “banger initial screen”) reads each post and outputs a description, tags, topic categories, yes/no flags like high quality, spam, and NSFW, and a “slop score.”
*   **The weights are in [`param.rs`](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/blob/main/home-mixer/params/param.rs).** A Copy-link share is incredibly valuable and worth a multiplier of 20, a reply is worth 5 (not 13.5 as past articles noted), quote 5, DM share 5, repost 1, and like 0.5. Getting reported is −234 and muting is −58.8 (so incredibly bad). Though note that these are based on _probabilities_ of actions, not actual actions themselves.
*   **A lot of the folk wisdom isn’t in the code.** There’s no weight for the author replying back, and I couldn’t find a Premium multiplier anywhere in the scoring code.
*   **Mutual follows got a big boost this summer.** Replies on original posts from mutual follows now count for 20 instead of 5 (X even published the [whole A/B test history](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/blob/main/docs/BIDIRECTIONAL_BOOST_CHANGE.md), which is pretty cool to see).

![Image 2: What each action is worth on X, as a multiplier on the predicted probability of each action: copy-link share 20, reply 5, quote 5, DM share 5, follow the author 4, repost 1, like 0.5, report minus 234, mute minus 58.8, not interested minus 43.2, block minus 31.2.](https://johnjwang.com/images/x-weights.svg)
## What this means for your posts

So what should you actually do?

1.   **Write things people send around.** A copy-link share carries 40 times the weight of a like, which makes it incredibly valuable. People generally tend to forward useful things like a surprising number, a clear chart, or an explanation that breaks something down simply.
2.   **Start conversations.** Replies and quotes each carry 10 times the weight of a like. Build mutual follows with people in your field, since their replies count four times as much.
3.   **Stay on topic.** To reach people who don’t follow you, your post has to land near their interests in embedding space. A post clearly about one thing gets a clear semantic ID.
4.   **Don’t rage bait.** Mutes and reports are by far the heaviest negative weights, so it’s not really in your interest to post baity content.
5.   **Post less, but better.** Your second post in someone’s feed counts at about 0.6x, and your third about 0.4x.
6.   **Everything expires in 48 hours.** The ranker stops considering older posts, so there’s definitely a timing element of a post and might make weekend vs weekday timing important (though how time plays a factor depends on viewing and posting distributions, which aren’t available in the code itself).
7.   **Links are fine now.** X [says the link penalty ended in mid-2025](https://www.freepressjournal.in/tech/x-product-head-nikita-bier-confirms-link-penalty-removed-over-a-year-ago-tells-mark-zuckerberg-he-can-post-them-directly), and the code agrees. Just make sure the post stands on its own.

There are still some things we don’t know, though. The trained model isn’t public and every score is personalized to the viewer, so you can’t compute ahead of time how a post will do, but it is pretty intersting to get this level of transparency on the algorithm.

kept.heading: AI MARKETING IS MOVING INTO THE DATA PLATFORM (14 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Agentic CDPs bring AI directly into governed customer data, giving agents the context needed to build audiences and design campaigns. Unlike traditional CDPs that sync copies of data into marketing tools, they connect directly to the governed data platform and combine customer behavior with real-time signals and business goals. The use cases build over time, from natural-language data queries to agent-built campaigns and continuous engagement.
kept.article_text:
Title: Issue #71 – The Agentic CDP

URL Source: https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-71-the-agentic-cdp-customerlake

Published Time: 2026-09-27T12:08:45+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Read time:** 14 minutes

**TL;DR**

*   **Agentic AI is still maturing for non-technical teams**; marketing will likely be the first to change as agents are **impacting the customer journey from both sides** (for research and purchasing, and to understand and engage those same customers).

*   CDPs are a great technology for marketing teams, but they are **middleware tools that usually sit outside the governed data estate** and were **not built with Agentic AI in mind**

*   An Agentic CDP is **completely embedded in the governed data platform, agent-first, and built with marketers in mind**. That combination creates “golden context” about your customers that agents are able to use to better understand, segment, and cater to customers

*   **Use cases build on each other** (from questions about governed data to campaign design to next-best action and continuous engagement), but buying the platform doesn’t move you up the maturity ladder; it just **means the ladder is there to climb**. So the foundations need to be there

If you believe LinkedIn, Substack, Google, influencers, etc., you would think Agentic AI is everywhere.

I would disagree.

In 2026, it has made incredible leaps, and [AI now writes a serious share of new code](https://www.elitebrains.com/blog/aI-generated-code-statistics-2025), solution development and other technical work. **But it still hasn’t properly cracked business domains.** I work with these people daily. Most are still **using AI as a chatbot**, while some have an email organizer or daily note routine. Maybe the odd person has built a few skills that are already months outdated.

The biggest reason for the gap is that **Agentic AI wasn’t built for marketers, finance directors, or operations professionals;** it was first built in the terminal (a term most business folk don’t know). Tech-savvy people could connect AI to their IDEs, spin up tasks against files scattered across their machine, and run agents on pre-scoped requirements. **This is intuitive for a data or tech person, but not for everyone else.**

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Hd2Z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9f433b40-6669-428f-a719-fce4a088372f_687x418.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Hd2Z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9f433b40-6669-428f-a719-fce4a088372f_687x418.png)

> Well, that reality is evolving, and it starts with the industry that brought data to the forefront 30-odd years ago—**marketing**!

This type of **innovation is taking the form of Agentic CDPs.** I partnered with [Databricks](https://www.databricks.com/?scid=701Vp00001CpGGDIA3&utm_medium=third-party&utm_source=dylan-anderson) to create this article for their new product [CustomerLake](https://www.databricks.com/product/customerlake-cdp?scid=701Vp00001CpGGDIA3&utm_medium=third-party&utm_source=dylan-anderson). As you know, I’m selective with sponsored partners, but I was excited about this one: I love Databricks and the ease of their tools, and this is a genuinely new approach to bridging the gap between data/AI and the business.

[Share](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-71-the-agentic-cdp-customerlake?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

_This article & newsletter is free (thanks to sponsors like [Databricks](https://www.databricks.com/?scid=701Vp00001CpGGDIA3&utm\_medium=third-party&utm\_source=dylan-anderson), which means passing it on is the only way it grows. If it was useful to you, it’s probably useful to someone on your team (especially the marketing function)._

My wife is a VP of Marketing at a decently sized scale-up. Her company is very AI-focused and using Claude all over the place. But despite my help and her company’s AI goals, **a huge gap remains between the value she gets from Agentic AI and what I get as a technical person.**

And the numbers back that up. McKinsey’s [State of AI](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai) says 23% of organizations are using an agentic system, with another 39% experimenting. But no more than 10% are scaling agents in any given business function, because that scaling remains confined to IT, data, service operations and software engineering.

> #### My wife fits in that 23%—using an agentic system but not scaling agents.

This divide comes down to two things:

1.   A lack of **technical understanding** to work effectively with Agentic AI

2.   A lack of**products built directly into how these professionals work**, therefore embedded into the workflow (I don’t count bolt-on AI features in this btw)

The other component is that companies are obsessed with productivity as the main value driver for AI. I’ve written about the [four opportunity areas of AI](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-59-ai-strategy): productivity gains are the lowest-hanging fruit, knowledge & context is the next rung up, and AI-enabled knowledge is what eventually creates growth.

[![Image 2: Four Opportunity Areas of AI](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bLgm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb0a4aec5-2492-4916-bbcd-74d6ee404fc3_1011x540.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bLgm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb0a4aec5-2492-4916-bbcd-74d6ee404fc3_1011x540.jpeg)

The point is that **very little AI investment is pointed at the company’s value proposition or growth; exactly the areas that the business owns**. Productivity only goes so far in marketing, finance or operations, and it’s incredibly hard to measure there anyway.

Despite all that, we are seeing **a shift in the industry where agents are changing how business teams work**. And that is no more apparent than in marketing.

It makes sense. Marketing is where d**ata science gained its popularity**: profiling customers, targeting segments, proving campaign value. Direct-mail segmentation in the seventies, loyalty programs in the 90s, then CRM, web analytics, the MarTech stack, and CDPs. Each of these involved data and reshaped how marketing teams worked.

What makes this wave different is that AI (and agents specifically) are making an impact from both directions at once:

*   **Customers** are using agents to research, compare, and increasingly transact

*   **Companies** are deploying agents to understand and engage those same customers

*   **Marketing infrastructure** now has to support both faster buyer behaviour and agent-operated internal workflows

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3kHb!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F10bf764c-3b7e-4b54-975c-cf6dceac1445_1438x832.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3kHb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F10bf764c-3b7e-4b54-975c-cf6dceac1445_1438x832.png)

_Agents are being used on both sides of the customer journey, something marketing teams need to now plan for and anticipate_

And the average buyer is probably using AI more than most marketing teams realize. According to CI&T research across 1,040 US consumers, [74% now use AI tools in their shopping journey](https://retailmediabreakfastclub.com/ai-shopping-hits-74-adoption/) at least occasionally. And it isn’t only chat interfaces; agents increasingly browse via APIs, which lets them research options, compare pricing, and purchase across more channels and far faster than any person clicking around. I mean [ChatGPT Ads hit $1 billion in annual run rate in 200 days](https://openai.com/index/expanding-access-to-ai-with-chatgpt-ads/), so obviously some marketing teams are starting to realize it…

This changes what marketing teams respond to. When a customer’s first pass at your category is an agent summarizing options rather than a person browsing them, the time to act shrinks, and you have to be far more attuned to your competitors.

So if marketing has been the entryway for every data wave, Agentic AI will be next, especially because marketers already use customer data daily for segmentation, personalization and campaigns.

[Share](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-71-the-agentic-cdp-customerlake?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

And the Customer Data Platform is a natural place for this evolution, given its role in connecting customer data to marketing action.

A Customer Data Platform [ingests and organizes customer data from the many places it exists across an organization](https://www.databricks.com/discover/enterprise-data-platform/cdp)—the website, app, CRM, transactional systems, social media, support tickets, etc. It resolves that into a **unified profile per person, letting marketers build audiences and push them into campaigns**. In plenty of companies, joining online browsing behaviour with in-store purchases and loyalty membership is effectively impossible. **A CDP brings those sources together**, builds a segment (say “lapsed high-value customer”), and streams it into a campaign without a request to the data team.

I’ve worked with a lot of marketing and sales teams, and doing this well was extremely difficult. Doing it as a data team, without a platform, was even harder. Data teams got caught up handling identity resolution across fragmented sources, directing data into activation tools, or just providing the right data when marketing needed it, usually on short notice.

So the CDP was a game changer for a lot of organizations. It provided:

*   Unified customer profiles

*   Data-driven segmentation of customers

*   Reverse ETL into activation tools and platforms

*   Accessible UI for research and insights

All of that was great; however, CDPs were never the perfect fix. They are **middleware**—sitting between the data platform, the MarTech stack, and the channels—and usually owned by marketing, so they **lived outside the governed data estate**. [Reverse ETL](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-35-business-value-reverse-etl) helped bridge the gap, but it synced a copy rather than live data.

Essentially, CDPs were built for marketing and activation, not for reasoning and data clarity. So they often lack the [modelled data](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-14-data-modelling) that keeps things consistent over time: defined grain, conformed dimensions, modelled relationships, lineage, and agreed business definitions.

> That was fine when humans reviewed the data, shaped the segments and crafted campaigns before manually activating.
> 
> 
> **It gets much harder with AI, especially if a marketing team wants agents handling personalized sends or campaign measurement** (and you know every exec aspires to that). The agent needs to know the customer definition, the campaign metrics, what counts as a churn event, the purchase cadence, and how all of it links together.

This all comes back to one growing problem in the AI world: the **lack of contextual data to map these things together.**

A CDP definitely helps because it at least stores this data in the same place. **Its biggest bottleneck is the middleware disconnect**. Now that we are in an AI world, a campaign-building agent may only get a representation of the data and context it needs because the CDP is disconnected from the primary data warehouse and the data team’s governance.

Worse still are organizations that don’t even have this middleware. Some use AI to reach from their harness (e.g., Claude, ChatGPT, etc.) directly into their data warehouse. This is dangerous because without proper governance and oversight, it **opens up a host of issues for the data team that owns and manages that data**. Especially when business stakeholders prompt AI to pull this or take a look at that, it becomes a security and management nightmare.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!koNd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F108c8d51-fef1-4c9e-a5de-c7669fcc0aa5_598x420.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!koNd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F108c8d51-fef1-4c9e-a5de-c7669fcc0aa5_598x420.jpeg)

> #### So many data teams simply don’t give marketing or sales access to the warehouse.

Again, I’ll reference my wife. As a VP of Marketing and avid AI user, she would love access to her Snowflake data warehouse. But she has no feasible route to it: there’s a technical gap in getting at it directly, no quality checks between the warehouse and her AI harness, and no architectural oversight of how she might use the data. She could request an MCP connection, but that hands a non-technical operator a raw pipe to production customer data. And while these warehouses support governed MCP access, it still takes a lot of data team resources to teach non-technical users and oversee their usage(and no data team has that kind of availability); ideally, a purpose-built application would be better.

This pattern worries me most when we talk about AI democratization. **Non-technical stakeholders don’t quite know what they are doing with their AI harness, but they are doing it ad hoc nonetheless.** Then the definitions drift, nothing is repeatable, and the whole thing goes stale. Or marketing builds its own thing because working with the data team is too slow, leading to a second version of the truth. That’s the risk with AI, and while CDPs were built to solve that kind of problem, they weren’t built with embedded AI in mind!

Technology comes in waves, with each iteration adding another layer to solve for new problems that have come about. Obviously, the most recent wave is AI…and more specifically Agentic AI.

In that vein, it also makes sense that these tools eventually reach the business domains. And as described above, marketing is a great candidate, with the CDP the most obvious first step.

[Share The Data & AI Ecosystem](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

An [Agentic CDP](https://www.databricks.com/blog/what-is-an-agentic-cdp) does three things:

1.   It is completely **embedded in the governed data platform**, rather than being copied and synced to a marketing tool, therefore giving it access to the data model, governance, and resources it needs to share the right insights.

2.   It is **agent-first**, treating Agentic operation as the primary mode of delivery for personalization, segmentation, campaign activation, etc.

3.   It’s **built with marketers in mind**, ensuring that the UI and UX is not a terminal-based agent swarm, but an accessible tool that non-technical people can use, built for their use cases.

Most CDPs on the market might say they’re agentic, but in reality, **they were built before ChatGPT existed, and most agentic capabilities are bolted on**, reducing their effectiveness. There is a real difference between adding a chat window to an existing tool and rebuilding the tool so agents are embedded in the workflows.

What does this enable from a business value perspective? Instead of just static records of customer data, this approach creates what [Scott Brinker](https://chiefmartec.com/) originally termed **“golden context”:** the overlap between your company’s goals, your customer’s needs, and your systems’ ability to deliver it in real time.

Say someone is shopping for running shoes on your site. The customer record tells you who they are: they bought a pair eighteen months ago, are size ten, spent about $140, and opted into email. This is useful information, and a good CDP will give this to you today.

But the golden context takes it to the next level. Beyond segmentation, golden context can provide size-level inventory data about the customer and show that they should have a contact-frequency limit based on their email interactions and how they purchase. No individual is realistically putting that together for each customer, but an agent embedded in the CDP should. And it might do it with the context that the company’s goal is to increase the rate of 2nd-time purchases, **so the agent prioritizes that in its marketing actions using the golden context.**

Context is such a buzzy word right now, but everyone agrees [it is the real moat for AI](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-60-context-layer-ai-needs). So imagine assembling all of that context about your customers and feeding it directly into your campaigns. That is what the Agentic CDP is after, and doing it at scale is becoming very real, very quickly.

But context is only powerful if you have the data to create it. And this is where the embedded nature of the Agentic CDP fits in—**you get the customer expertise from the marketing team integrated with the customer data of the warehouse, all in one tool.**

[Share](https://thedataecosystem.substack.com/p/issue-71-the-agentic-cdp-customerlake?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

For most companies, your customer data is the most valuable data you have on hand. Loyalty behaviour, purchase patterns, lifetime value, and churn signals are the data points that decide whether you keep a customer or lose them. And while this is no surprise, that data is also among the worst quality: records go stale, identities fragment across tools and definitions don’t agree.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oLo8!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F57086417-5fc3-4237-9e17-b91560c67ad3_1288x804.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oLo8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F57086417-5fc3-4237-9e17-b91560c67ad3_1288x804.png)

_Going from middleware to embedded with agentic capabilities will make a big difference for marketing teams_

The beauty of Databricks is that they’ve been solving this data access, governance and quality question for years (and made a pretty big name of themselves doing it), so [CustomerLake translates well into this type of architecture](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-customerlake-agentic-cdp?scid=701Vp00001CpGGDIA3&utm_medium=third-party&utm_source=dylan-anderson). Either way, this is what I would want to see for Agentic CDPs to make sure marketing teams get the benefit they need:

*   **Governance and PII in One Place** – Customer data needs to be governed well, especially given the PII risks or GDPR rules. Every MarTech tool you copy customer data into becomes another surface to secure, audit, and honour deletion requests against. Removing copies streamlines how you govern that data. [CustomerLake](https://www.databricks.com/product/customerlake-cdp?scid=701Vp00001CpGGDIA3&utm_medium=third-party&utm_source=dylan-anderson) runs this through [Unity Catalog](https://www.databricks.com/product/unity-catalog), which, if you already use Databricks, is likely the governance layer running the rest of your estate already

*   **Data Quality Built In** – Any CDP worth its price should do identity resolution. But if schemas change in the warehouse, that doesn’t always translate across, and engineering pipelines can break. This is the data-readiness piece. An agentic system needs to combine the [preparation of data](https://www.databricks.com/dataaisummit/session/introducing-customerlake-profile-agents) by identifying quality issues, enriching records and creating business-ready profiles with [agentic identity resolution](https://www.databricks.com/blog/introducing-customerlake-agentic-cdp?scid=701Vp00001CpGGDIA3&utm_medium=third-party&utm_source=dylan-anderson), which combines deterministic, probabilistic, agentic and human-review workflows rather than betting everything on a single matching method. Sounds like a lot but data quality is essential and agents plugged into the business data warehouse are perfectly positioned to do this with the right context

*   **Natural Language Access** – The future is not SQL queries; it is natural language guiding those queries. So the tool needs features where a business user describes what they need in their own language and gets something they can act on (for Databricks and CustomerLake, this is [their Genie tool](https://www.databricks.com/product/genie/agents)). Honestly, this would be the first thing my wife would want from her MarTech tooling

*   **Auditing and Troubleshooting** – Testing and reconciliation only really works when activation tools are properly connected to the warehouse. So if a campaign misfires (the wrong segment goes out, the numbers don’t reconcile, the product isn’t linked properly), working out why is cumbersome and manual, meaning it rarely happens. An agentic CDP should query the campaign, audit what went wrong using its [embedded data and lineage function](https://www.databricks.com/product/unity-catalog), and set guardrails so it doesn’t happen again

*   **Connection Without Migration** – Saving the best for last. Migration is a bad word in any company. Your new CDP should plug into the data platform you already own, which Databricks handles through [Lakehouse Federation](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-federated-queries), reading across Snowflake, BigQuery and operational databases. But it also has to plug into the MarTech and AdTech stack you already run, through Reverse ETL integrations out to your email, ad and CX platforms. Doing both a MarTech and data migration to connect a CDP is why many implementations take more time than planned. So whoever you go with, figure out the solutions architecture on both sides before signing anything

When AI Agents can work directly with governed customer data in a tool the marketing team knows how to use, everything becomes easier. This is the advantage of embedded AI, and this is how you actually make Agentic AI scale to non-data and tech functions.

Coming back to the four areas of AI opportunity I mentioned earlier (productivity, knowledge & context, new products or tools, and growth opportunities), the embedded nature of the Agentic CDP lets you start capturing value beyond productivity:

kept.heading: THE STACK LADDER: WHAT COMPANIES RUN AT 10, 50, 200, 1,000, AND 10,000 PEOPLE (9 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Startups don't necessarily switch to enterprise software as they grow. Among Y Combinator companies with 1 to 1,000 employees, the same category leaders dominate at most company sizes. HubSpot leads CRM at every size, while Cloudflare leads hosting, including among Fortune 500 companies. Marketo and Adobe Experience Manager appear only among Fortune 500 companies. What changes with headcount is adoption. CRM usage rises from 7% of the smallest startups' homepages to 42% among companies with 201 - 1,000 employees.

Title: The stack ladder: what companies run at 10, 50, 200, 1,000 and 10,000 people

URL Source: https://installmap.com/research/software-stack-by-company-size

Published Time: 2026-09-27
