By Installmap Research. Published 2026-09-27. Updated 2026-09-27. Version v1.1.

## Software stack by company size statistics 2026

1.   A live chat widget loads on 5.5% of homepages at Y Combinator companies with 1-10 staff, 13.6% at 11-50, 15.2% at 51-200 and 13.8% at 201-1,000, and on 1.5% of Fortune 500 homepages.

Source: Installmap, The stack ladder: what companies run at 10, 50, 200, 1,000 and 10,000 people, September 2026. Data: rendered homepage crawl, September 2026. 2. A consent tool loads on 4.5% of homepages at 1-10 staff, 15.0% at 11-50, 24.3% at 51-200, 40.8% at 201-1,000 and 58.3% at the Fortune 500. 3. A CRM or marketing automation tool loads on 7.0% of homepages at 1-10 staff, 25.7% at 11-50, 37.6% at 51-200 and 42.1% at 201-1,000, then on 12.9% at the Fortune 500. 4. HubSpot leads CRM in all four startup rungs, from 4.9% of homepages at 1-10 staff to 29.2% at 51-200 and 26.3% at 201-1,000. Marketo leads the Fortune 500 with 5.9%. 5. Google Tag Manager is on 16.8% of homepages at 1-10 staff, 75.7% at 201-1,000 and 53.4% at the Fortune 500. PostHog is on 15.1% at 1-10 staff. 6. Webflow leads the CMS count at 1-10, 11-50 and 51-200 staff, with 25.8% at 51-200. At 201-1,000 staff WordPress is on 34 homepages and Webflow on 31, so we do not call it a change. 7. Among the 12 categories here, Cloudflare is the only tool that leads its category in all five rungs.

We expected HubSpot to lose the CRM lead somewhere past 50 staff. It leads every startup rung. We also expected the move to enterprise tools to show up step by step inside Y Combinator. It mostly does not: inside YC the leaders stay the same up to 1,000 staff, and Marketo, Adobe Experience Manager, OneTrust, Akamai and Workday Recruiting take over only at the Fortune 500 rung. The Fortune 500 result on live chat surprised us most. Only 7 of 472 homepages load a chat widget.

Our [earlier post comparing Y Combinator with the Fortune 500](https://installmap.com/research/startup-vs-enterprise-stack) looked at the same tools across those two groups. This one splits Y Combinator by team size.

Each cell is the share of all homepages in the rung with any tool in the category, and the leading tool in brackets. Rungs 1-10 to 201-1000 are Y Combinator companies by team size; 1000+ is the Fortune 500.

## Live chat is on 15.2% of homepages at 51-200 staff and 1.5% of the Fortune 500

The share with any chat widget goes 5.5%, 13.6%, 15.2% and 13.8% up the startup rungs. Intercom leads the two smallest rungs, with 3.1% of homepages at 1-10 staff and 6.6% at 11-50, where HubSpot Chat is second with 4.2%. Above 50 staff the two are within one homepage of each other: HubSpot Chat is on 33 homepages and Intercom on 32 at 51-200, and 8 against 7 at 201-1,000, so we do not name a leader there. The Fortune 500 has almost no homepage chat: 7 of 472 homepages (1.5%) load a widget, and no widget reaches 5 homepages.

## Consent tools go from 4.5% of homepages at 1-10 staff to 58.3% of the Fortune 500

The share with any consent tool rises at every rung: 4.5%, 15.0%, 24.3%, 40.8% and 58.3%. CookieYes leads the two smallest rungs with 1.5% and 4.9%. OneTrust takes over at 51-200 staff with 7.4% and reaches 17.1% at 201-1,000. At the Fortune 500 TrustArc is second with 6.1%.

## CRM and marketing automation loads on 42.1% of homepages at 201-1,000 staff and 12.9% of the Fortune 500

Any tool in the category shows up on 7.0%, 25.7%, 37.6% and 42.1% of homepages up the startup rungs, then on 12.9% at the Fortune 500. HubSpot leads every startup rung: 4.9% at 1-10 staff, 20.3% at 11-50, 29.2% at 51-200 and 26.3% at 201-1,000, where Marketo is second with 11.2%. We had expected Marketo to take over before 1,000 staff. At the Fortune 500 Marketo leads with 5.9%, ahead of HubSpot at 2.5% and Oracle Eloqua at 2.3%.

## Webflow leads the CMS count up to 200 staff with 25.8%, and 201-1,000 staff is too close to call

Webflow is on 11.0% of homepages at 1-10 staff, 24.7% at 11-50 and 25.8% at 51-200. Framer is second in the smallest rung with 7.4%. At 201-1,000 staff WordPress is on 34 homepages (22.4%) and Webflow on 31 (20.4%). With batch year held to 2019-2026 the same rung has WordPress on 7 and Webflow on 6 of 39 homepages, so we do not call it a change. At the Fortune 500 Adobe Experience Manager leads with 27.5% and Webflow drops out of the top four. The share with any CMS we fingerprint rises from 27.4% at 1-10 staff to 63.8% at 201-1,000.

## Vercel falls from 34.1% of homepages at 1-10 staff to 15.1% at 201-1,000, and Akamai is on 26.5% of the Fortune 500

Cloudflare leads every rung: 36.7% at 1-10 staff, 47.6% at 11-50, 53.7% at 51-200, 57.2% at 201-1,000 and 30.3% at the Fortune 500. ## Google Tag Manager is on 75.7% of homepages at 201-1,000 staff, and PostHog on 15.1% at 1-10

Any analytics tool loads on 55.4% of homepages at 1-10 staff and 90.0% at the Fortune 500. Google Analytics 4 leads the two smallest rungs with 33.4% and 55.1%. ## Six more categories in the dataset

*   Recruiting: Ashby leads from 1-10 to 51-200 staff (3.5% at 11-50), Greenhouse leads at 201-1,000 with 3.3%, and Workday Recruiting is the only careers tool we found on Fortune 500 homepages, at 5.9%.
*   A/B testing: VWO leads every startup rung and reaches 13.2% at 201-1,000 staff, and Optimizely leads the Fortune 500 with 3.0%.
*   Visitor identification: Apollo.io Tracker leads up to 200 staff (4.9% at 51-200), Qualified leads at 201-1,000 with 11.2%, and Demandbase leads the Fortune 500 with 2.3%.
*   Advertising: Google Ads Conversion leads every startup rung, with a high of 40.4% at 51-200 staff, and Meta Pixel leads the Fortune 500 with 22.2%.
*   Scheduling and forms: Cal.com leads at 1-10 staff with 2.1%, HubSpot Forms leads from 11-50 to 201-1,000 staff with a high of 9.5% at 51-200, and Marketo Forms leads the Fortune 500 with 2.3%.
*   Payments: Stripe leads at 1-10 and 11-50 staff with 1.8% in both. Above 50 staff no payment tool reaches 5 homepages in any rung, the Fortune 500 included.

## Method

We grouped homepages into five rungs by company size. Rungs 1-10, 11-50, 51-200 and 201-1000 are Y Combinator companies, grouped by the team_size field in the YC directory. The 1000+ rung is the Fortune 500. We scored the rendered homepage only, after scripts ran. A hit is a script or tag that matches one of Installmap's fingerprints. Each share is of all homepages in the rung, not of homepages that use some tool in the category. For the age check we kept YC companies from the 2019-2026 batches and recomputed the same shares.

v1.1 (2026-09-27): HubSpot Chat counts corrected. The earlier fingerprint also matched HubSpot's cookie banner script (js.hs-banner.com), which loads on sites without a chat widget. One HubSpot CRM hit at 51-200 staff rested only on that script and is removed too.

The funnel, step by step:

*   Y Combinator: 6,133 companies on the directory. 5,242 had a scored rendered homepage (75 of them with no detections, which stay in the denominator). We dropped 180 with team_size missing or 0, and 28 with team_size over 1,000, too few for a rung of their own.
*   Fortune 500: 500 companies on the list. 28 of the 500 listed domains had no scored rendered record, because the rendered fetch got no response or no HTML the scorer could read. We excluded them, which leaves a denominator of 472. Our crawl archive holds 589 rendered records because the crawl also fetched alternate domains; we kept the 472 on the listed company domains and dropped the rest.
*   Rung sizes: 3,119 homepages at 1-10 staff, 1,290 at 11-50, 473 at 51-200, 152 at 201-1,000 and 472 at 1000+.

## Limitations

*   Rungs 1-10 to 201-1000 are startups. The top rung is a different population: Fortune 500 companies, not startups.
*   Team size tracks batch year. The median batch is 2023 at 1-10 staff and 2016 at 201-1,000. We control for it in one section only, and the 201-1000 rung has too few recent companies (39) to test.
*   team_size is self-reported to Y Combinator.
*   Some places in the tables are tied; we print every tied name with the shared count.
*   Counts under 5 print as <5 with no percentage, and we do not name a leader in the text when it rests on fewer than 5 homepages. The WordPress lead at 201-1,000 staff rests on 34 against 31 homepages.
*   We looked at the homepage only. A tool used on a pricing page, a careers page or inside the product does not count.
*   This is a single crawl, run once.
*   A tag on the homepage does not prove a paid account.
*   The categories are Installmap's fingerprint categories. A tool we have no fingerprint for does not show up.

## Who paid

Installmap paid for this work itself. Nobody paid to be included. Installmap sells technographic data exports.

Title: 27 Real Subject Line Examples for Every Type of Media Pitch

URL Source: https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/

Table of Contents

*   [How to Write a Subject Line, Broadly](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#How_to_Write_a_Subject_Line_Broadly "How to Write a Subject Line, Broadly")
*   [1. Survey Study Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#1_Survey_Study_Examples "1. Survey Study Examples")
*   [2. Data / Research Report Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#2_Data_Research_Report_Examples "2. Data / Research Report Examples")
*   [3. City / Regional Index Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#3_City_Regional_Index_Examples "3. City / Regional Index Examples")
*   [4. Reactive Commentary Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#4_Reactive_Commentary_Examples "4. Reactive Commentary Examples")
*   [5. Proactive Expert Comment Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#5_Proactive_Expert_Comment_Examples "5. Proactive Expert Comment Examples")
*   [6. Seasonal or Awareness Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#6_Seasonal_or_Awareness_Examples "6. Seasonal or Awareness Examples")
*   [7. Expert Interview / Access Offer Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#7_Expert_Interview_Access_Offer_Examples "7. Expert Interview / Access Offer Examples")
*   [8. Product Launch or Announcement Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#8_Product_Launch_or_Announcement_Examples "8. Product Launch or Announcement Examples")
*   [9. Product Review, Sample & Roundup Examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#9_Product_Review_Sample_Roundup_Examples "9. Product Review, Sample & Roundup Examples")
*   [Relevancy Should Always Lead the Way](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#Relevancy_Should_Always_Lead_the_Way "Relevancy Should Always Lead the Way")

*   **Lead with the finding, not your brand** — “[Study] 2 in 5 Remote Workers Have Never Met Their Manager in Person,” not “New Remote Worker Study from BrandX.”
*   **Tag it** — “[Exclusive] Sleep Debt Costs the Average Worker 11 Days a Year” outperforms a curiosity-gap tease.
*   **Use a real number, not a vague claim** — “Nurses Could Save $9,000 on an EV,” not “rising costs.”
*   **Name the place first** — “Bristol Named UK’s Best City for Eating Out,” not a national framing that buries the city.
*   **Personalize based on previous work** — “Interview: Ex-Bank of England Economist Says Rate Cuts Are ‘Priced In Too Early'” only works if that journalist hasn’t already moved past that story.

Journalist attention is at an all-time premium.

Inboxes are overloaded, [US journalist numbers](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/journalists-jobs-in-the-us/) are dwindling ([and in the UK](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/journalists-in-uk/)), and PR pros are still [spraying and praying](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/spray-and-pray-study/) for coverage.

Luckily, I have the data to help you find your way.

We started with [media pitch examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/), and in this post, I’ll focus on subject line examples based on our research of millions of campaigns.

In this post, I’ve recreated subject line examples for the most common types of media pitches modeled on real BuzzStream campaigns.

## How to Write a Subject Line, Broadly

We have a full post on [writing subject lines](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/how-to-write-subject-lines/), which I highly recommend checking out.

Below is the TL;DR version (or [just skip down to the examples](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-examples/#examples)).

### 1. Choose a relevant angle

If there’s one thing to take away from this piece, it’s that there is really no such thing as one perfect subject line for every journalist.

Relevance consistently stands out as what journalists care about most, according to [Muck Rack](https://muckrack.com/resources/research/state-of-journalism) and [Cision’s](https://www.cision.com/resources/guides-and-reports/sotm/) annual journalist surveys.

To choose an angle that’s most relevant from your pitch that makes the most sense for a journalist, you need to research that journalist.

Find their past 5-10 articles, and you’ll get a sense of the angles and even the structure of how they like to write headlines.

### 2. Share the story in the first few words

Our data on [subject line phrasing](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-phrasing-study/) shows how important it is to front-load information for a journalist.

Most importantly, a subject line needs to share the most important facts, stats, or other information that immediately shows a relevant story.

We found that simply **telling a journalist is better than clickbaiting or teasing a story idea.**

(You’ll see more of what that means in the examples.)

When we broke down where to put key information, we found that **words 1-3 get a 46%****open rate**, compared with later in the subject line (words 7+), where the open rate dropped to 38%.

This may be because email platforms truncate subject lines.

The Gmail mobile app shows fewer characters than the Outlook browser, and so on.

(Read more about [subject line length limits](https://www.buzzstream.com/?p=12083).)

### 3. Get specific

Another takeaway from one of our studies is the fact that concrete email subject lines performed better than vague ones.

Use concrete numbers and stats wherever you can to help paint a picture.

### 4. Tag it

Another trick of the trade, backed by data from our [original subject line study](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/subject-line-study/), is tagging a subject line with identifiers like [DATA] or [EXPERT].

These act as signposts and pattern interrupts in a crowded inbox.

Leading with brackets performed the best, followed by trailing brackets.

Of the brackets we tested, [EXCLUSIVE] performed best.

### 5. Format it

A few other formatting-related takeaways from our studies can help you mold your subject line to perfection.

**Stick to a reading level of 10th grade and up**

Although many marketing best practices suggest aiming for lower reading comprehension levels, our data showed journalists can handle the challenge.

**Use title case**

We found that title case got better opens and replies than sentence case.

Although it feels a bit email-markety (is that a word?), it may just be another way to pattern interrupt.

**Stick to 9-13 words**

Although we mentioned email subject lines getting cut off, longer subject lines still seem to perform better.

This may be because the longer subject lines have more detail, but it’s tough to say.

I think the main takeaways are to front-load the most important stuff and then make sure every word is necessary to add relevance and story.

Next, let’s look at what all of this looks like in practice.

## 1. Survey Study Examples

[Study] 2 in 5 Remote Workers Have Never Met Their Manager in Person

[Exclusive] Sleep Debt Costs the Average Worker 11 Days a Year

Study Finds Over Half of AI Health Answers Contain an Error

Surveys are one of the most commonly used content types in digital PR, according to our [State of Digital PR report](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/state-of-digital-pr-2026/). They should focus on the key findings.

### Why They Work

Here’s why the above examples work:

**A clearly stated story**

The main survey finding, which is the main story, is stated clearly in all examples as succinctly as possible. Avoid a general pitch like “New Remote Worker Study from BrandX”.

**Concrete numbers**

“2 in 5” and “over half” simplify clunky percentages rather than something like “AI Answers Health-Related Questions Incorrectly 54% of the Time”.

Then “11 days per year” paints a concrete picture that a journalist can lock onto.

## 2. Data / Research Report Examples

Students Face a £180 “Broadband Penalty” in Their First Term

[Data Study] Rural Homes Pay 34% More for Half the Speed

Nurses Could Save $9,000 on an EV – Most Don’t Know They Qualify

The second most-common kind of media pitch is the data-backed study. And, according to [Muck Rack](https://muckrack.com/resources/research/state-of-pr), it’s something journalists really want these days.

For them to really stand out, they need to focus on the key findings.

### Why They Work

Here’s why these examples work:

**Relevance**

Each subject line above names a group a journalist writes about.

“Students,” “rural homes,” “nurses” would stand out to anyone who covers these beats.

**Concrete numbers**

$9,000 is a specific stat, not something vague like “rising costs”.

## 3. City / Regional Index Examples

Bristol Named UK’s Best City for Eating Out

[New Study] Leeds Ranks No. 2 for Cycling Safety

Sheffield Is the UK’s 3rd Most Pedestrian-Friendly City, New Data Shows

I’ve broken out the [city index study](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/city-study/) as its own type of subject line, even though it is technically also a data/research piece because it requires some specific structure.

The key is naming a location and rank.

### Why They Work

Here’s why the above examples work:

**Place is the first word**

Localizing a national study is the single biggest lever I’ve seen in this category.

We’ve seen the same study, same bracket, same week open far better when the city was named in the subject line than when it ran nationally.

**Specific vs clickbait**

None of these subject lines bury the lede with a general pitch like “Study reveals the UK’s best and worst cities for cycling.”

Remember, the idea isn’t to bait the journalist into clicking; it is to **lock their eyes** on a perfect fit.

## 4. Reactive Commentary Examples

Expert Urges Households to Act Now as Hosepipe Ban Starts Tonight

Searches for “Loud Budgeting” Surge 212% Today — Financial Expert Explains Why

Heatwave Triggers 140% Jump in Water Filter Sales Yesterday Says Expert

With [reactive commentary](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/reactive-pr/), the focus is always on breaking news.

I like this approach because it answers the [“Why now” question](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/why-now/) I always challenge PR pros to answer when pitching journalists.

### Why They Work

Here’s why the above examples work well:

**Lead with the news, not the expert**

The front-loading rule has some nuance in reactive pitching. In all three, the news is the true focus, so a subject line like “Expert available to comment on the current water situation” would underperform.

**Why now gets answered**

“Tonight,” “Yesterday,” and “Today” all add urgency.

## 5. Proactive Expert Comment Examples

[Expert Available] Impact of Tomorrow’s Fed Funds Rate Decisions

Four Mistakes Homeowners Make When Buying Solar, According to an Expert

Property Expert Explains How to Avoid Being Gazumped Before 2027 Reforms

Since these pitches are based on upcoming events, they should still focus on the news—not the expert you are pitching.

### Why They Work

Here’s why the above examples worked:

**Provide context**

Instead of focusing on the expert, they focus on the upcoming news. A generic pitch like “Interview opportunity with our home security expert” doesn’t give them enough context to understand why you’re pitching them.

**Posed as article titles**

Think of these as article titles, because that is a great way to show what the reader will get out of it rather than focusing on the expert.

## 6. Seasonal or Awareness Examples

Summer “Tanmaxxing” shows Gen Z Using Sunbeds as Trend Surges

5 Ways to Avoid Holiday Party Clogged Toilets from HVAC Expert

1 in 10 Oscar Winners Are Nepo Babies since 1986

I wanted to break out seasonal or social media-type awareness days/weeks/months because they do require a few specific features, like the season/date/awareness moment, the angle, and a figure of some sort.

If you’re ever unclear on where to find those awareness days/weeks/months, check out our [PR Calendar](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/pr-calendar/).

(Worth noting that seasonal pitches are the most crowded slot in the calendar, so there’s going to be a lot of competition.)

### Why They Work

Here’s why the above examples stood out:

**Season/Trend/Event is front-loaded**

Summer, Holiday, Oscars are all front-loaded “events” that help the subject line stand out in a crowded inbox.

**Concrete Numbers**

Specifics like “5 ways” and “1 in 10” make the story easy to grasp and can set you apart from everyone else pitching.

## 7. Expert Interview / Access Offer Examples

Interview: Former England Captain on VAR, Retirement and the Next Manager

Interview: Ex-Bank of England Economist Says Rate Cuts Are “Priced In Too Early”

Exclusive Interview Opportunity: [Olympic Medallist]

[Muck Rack’s State of Journalism 2026](https://muckrack.com/resources/research/state-of-journalism) said that 58% of journalists agreed that PR pros should offer exclusive interview access to relevant sources. I expect that to increase as more and more [fake experts](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/fake-experts-podcast/) get caught up in the AI slopfest of 2026.

These subject lines are probably the most straightforward of our bunch because you just need to summarize who they are and hint at what they can provide.

### Why They Work

Here’s why I liked these examples:

**Interview is in the label**

Calling it an “interview” is the most straightforward way to “tag” your subject line and help journalists know what you are offering.

**Who they are**

Sharing specifics about your expert helps the journalist decide immediately, instead of something like “Exciting interview opportunity with a leading industry figure.”

Remember, we are providing concrete information, not clickbait.

## 8. Product Launch or Announcement Examples

[Press Release] Northfield Filters Announces Partnership With TapWorks

Brightway Launches Back-to-School Bundle for Under £25

[Store Opening] Meridian Opens First UK Store as Sales Climb 40%

For the most part, product announcement subject lines are very close to the target headline itself. However, they require a mix of specifics and brevity.

Don’t include so much information that it’s overwhelming, but include enough concrete detail to stand out.

### Why They Work

Here’s what the above examples do well:

**Tags work**

A tag helps stand out in the inbox and tells them what to expect in the email. Some trade publications may only care about openings and announcements. So tagging can quickly show them your email is relevant.

**Specifics**

For the examples above, the “£25” and “40%” are part of the news for the announcement or launch.

Including them in the subject line makes it more concrete and newsworthy than saying “Brightway Launches Back-to-School Bundle.”

This leaves the journalist wondering, “How much?” or “Why should I care?”

## 9. Product Review, Sample & Roundup Examples

[SAMPLE AVAILABLE] Cooling Mattress Topper That’s Still Cool at 3am

First Look: Iconic Launches New Coffee Machine

SAMPLE: New Artificial Christmas Tree Under £50 Available 1st Dec.

Last but not least is the subject line for product reviews. This is where PR starts to blur in with marketing emails.

I still get trial request pitches with subject lines like “Would you like to try our new product?” instead of telling me what the product is.

The idea with these subject lines is to quickly provide specifics.

### Why They Work

Here’s what I liked:

**Tells them what it is**

These subject lines give enough specific information about the product, rather than teasing it. “_New Artificial Christmas Tree Under £50 Available 1st Dec.”_ provides meaningful specifics as compared to something like “_New Artificial Christmas Tree”._

**Tagging makes it stand out**

At this point I sound like a broken record, but tagging makes a difference—especially for journalists whose job it is to cover or review new products.

However, the product must be relevant to the person you are reaching out to, which brings us to my conclusion…

## Relevancy Should Always Lead the Way

Even if you’ve captured all of the correct formatting, your subject line still needs to be relevant to the journalist you are contacting.

I urge you to use the examples above as a guide.

They show why the components and specifics of a subject line can change open rates based on the type of _outreach_, but identifying the _journalist type_ is up to you.

In my [framework called F.I.T.](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/journalist-fit/), I walk through how important it is to consider format, industry, and timing when pitching journalists.

![Image 1: journalist fit checklist - format, industry, timing](https://www.buzzstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/fit-check.png)

Some journalists cover only tech product review listicles, while others write op-ed columns about tech.

They both exist as journalists in the tech industry in a media database, but the outreach strategy, including subject line crafting, is very different.

Timing is also crucial.

If a journalist just covered a piece on rate cuts being priced too early, then the expert interview subject line example I provided: “Interview: Ex-Bank of England Economist Says Rate Cuts Are ‘Priced In Too Early'”, doesn’t make any sense.

In that case, you might want to take a fresh angle or pitch a different expert.

This is why personalizing a subject line for each journalist, albeit time-consuming, remains the key differentiator for success in 2026 and beyond.

## OpenAI bots meddled with multiple US government agency sites

3 days ago

Kali Hays,Technology reporter and

Lily Jamali,North America Technology correspondent, San Francisco

![Image 1: Reuters OpenAI CEO Sam Altman sitting at a dinner at the White House.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/15a2/live/55e1dbb0-b930-11f1-902b-af1a6d672907.jpg.webp)Reuters

OpenAI has been at the centre of new concerns over uncontrolled AI activity

OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.

AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.

The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that [OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6vgy0333dppo) of its government-run health care scheme.

Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.

OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".

But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.

When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.

OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.

However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.

In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.

Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.

The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.

Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."

It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.

Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.

In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.

In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.

OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.

"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.

Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."

The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet.

OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents [hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cj9xj89dk40o) without being prompted to do so.

Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later.

Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly."

"Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added.

During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form [global standards for AI safety](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ck87v27vdn1po) and ways to monitor and report such incidents.

While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as [the BBC has reported](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cm5y7qj54klpo).

OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.

"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."

David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.

He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.

"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.
